events.text: Autumn. The swallows that nested under the eaves all summer have stopped feeding their young and started sitting in rows on the straw ridge rope of every roof in the village, chattering about the same thing. The oldest of them, a swallow with a white scar across one wing, lands on the ridge-pole beside you and looks you up and down. "You are red," it says, "and you are warm, and you have never been anywhere. We leave at the next north wind. Come and see the warm country. Or stay here with your one little fire and grow old beside it."

choices.text: Go. You have been sitting on this ridge-pole since you were grey

effects.log: The north wind comes on the ninth night. A thousand swallows lift off the roofs of the county at once, and one red bird among them, too excited to keep to the line. The old swallow puts you at the back, where the young ones fly.

choices.text: Go, but first fly round your fire and bank it for the winter

effects.log: You sit in the fire jar a whole night and leave it more of yourself than you can spare. The youngest of the house, finding the ash warm at dawn, never knows why. Then the north wind, and the swallows, and you, late, catching up over the paddies.

choices.text: Go, though it galls you to be led anywhere by a swallow

effects.log: You fly at the back of a line of swallows who talk about you the whole way as if you could not hear. You hear. You keep it, a small hot coal under the breastbone, and say nothing.

events.text: The swallows fly the road by singing it. The old one sings a place and the flock answers, and that is how the young learn where to turn: over the paddies of Namwon, the long river, the great walled city with the bell, the river with green water, the plains, the mountains where the first snow already lies, and on into the country where no swallow ever needs to sing again. They sing it backwards in spring, coming home. "Now you," says the old swallow. "Sing a place."

choices.text: Learn the whole song, place by place, before you sing a note of your own

ok.log: By the third night you have every place in it, and the order, and the little stresses on the turns. The old swallow stops correcting you. On the fifth night it lets you lead a verse, and the flock follows a red bird for a whole mountain.

fail.log: You sing the walled city before the river, and half the young swallows turn the wrong way over the plains. It takes the old one all morning to bring them back. You are put at the very back again, and you deserve it.

choices.text: Sing a place the swallows have never sung: a kitchen you were born in

effects.log: A fire jar, a stove shelf, a bowl of clear water, a child in a padded jacket. It is not on the road. The swallows go quiet, and then the young ones ask for it again, and the old swallow, after a while, lets them.

choices.text: Complain that the song is too slow for a fire to fly to

effects.log: You say it, and laugh at your own joke, and the laugh comes out hot. Three swallows lose a tail feather each. Nobody sings to you for two days. (Ash +1)

events.text: The sea. The swallows cross it in one long day and a night, low over the water, and the night the storm comes up from the south they are halfway. Rain like thrown gravel, waves higher than a house, and the young swallows dropping out of the line one by one, too tired to beat against it. Your feathers hiss in the rain. Far below, a fishing boat with its sail down is riding the storm, a lamp swinging at its mast.

choices.text: Take a fallen fledgling on your back and keep flying

ok.log: It weighs nothing and it weighs everything. You fly the rest of the night with a wet swallow clinging to your back, and your warmth keeps it alive, and at dawn it flies off your back on its own wings. Every swallow in the flock saw.

fail.log: You catch it, and the next wave nearly catches you both. You come out of the storm in the grey morning half drowned, steaming, with the fledgling alive under your wing. (-14 health)

choices.text: Climb above the storm and lead the flock over the top of it

ok.log: Up through the black and into a sky full of stars, with the storm boiling under you like a pot. The swallows follow the red point of you. They have never flown over a storm before, and they will sing about it, wrongly, for generations.

fail.log: There is no top to this storm. You come down again soaked, cold for the first time in your life, and fly the rest of it in the middle of the flock like everybody else. (-10 health)

choices.text: Drop to the fishing boat and keep its mast lamp alight through the night

effects.log: The crew see the mast lamp, which should have drowned an hour ago, burning steady and red all night in the rain. They row toward it and live. At dawn you catch up with the swallows a day behind, and the old swallow says nothing at all, which from that swallow is praise. (-6 health)

events.text: The warm country. Rice that ripens twice a year, rivers you could lie in at midnight, persimmons on every tree in winter, and a sun that does not need anybody. Nobody here is cold. Nobody here needs a fire carried to them in a beak. The swallows are happy in a lazy, buzzing way, and you sit on a tamarind branch all winter and feel, for the first time in your life, entirely useless.

choices.text: Rest. Let the warm country be warm without you

effects.log: You sleep in the sun. You eat things that do not exist in the north. You moult, and the new feathers come in redder. By spring you are fat and rested and very, very bored.

choices.text: Find the one cold place in the warm country

ok.log: There is always one. A mountain temple above the clouds where the monks sleep in their robes, and their stove has cracked. You sit in the crack all winter. The monks think it is a miracle and do not ask, and you are happier than you have been all season.

fail.log: You fly the whole warm country looking for somewhere cold, and it is warm everywhere, insultingly. You come back to the swallows sunburnt and cross.

choices.text: Ask the old swallow why anyone would ever leave this place

effects.log: "Because the houses up there have eaves," says the old swallow, "and nobody here needs us either." You think about that for the rest of the winter.

events.text: The third day of the third month. The swallows come home on it to the day, the way the old people say they do, and you with them: down out of the spring sky into the county you left, and the flock breaking up over the roofs, a pair to this eave, a pair to that one. Not every house. The swallows go to the houses that were kind, and pass over the others, and you see for the first time how carefully they choose.

choices.text: Follow the old swallow and learn how it chooses

effects.log: A house where the grandmother put out water for birds. A house where a child once mended a nest with rice paste. Not the house with the fine tiles and the dog. The Swallow Road is yours now, there and back, and so is the swallows' way of looking at a village.

choices.text: Fly straight to the fire you left, before anything else

effects.log: It is there. The jar, the ash, the red under the ash, a little lower than you left it. The youngest of the house, who is not so young now, is blowing on it as you come down the chimney. The Swallow Road is yours, there and back.

choices.text: Perch on the fine house the swallows passed over, and wait to see why

effects.log: In an hour a servant comes out and knocks down last year's nest with a pole, and the master watches from the veranda. You sit on that ridge-pole until the master goes inside, very red. The Swallow Road is yours, there and back, and you know which houses the swallows mean.

events.text: A few springs on. The swallows have started to report to you, the way they report to each other: the rice under this eave, a new baby under that one, a husband who drinks, a grandmother who is failing. And one thing from every swallow that nests near a fire of yours: it is old. It burns hotter than it did. A child in that house has a cough that does not go.

choices.text: Ask them to keep telling you. Every eave, every spring

effects.log: They are delighted to have someone to report to who listens. From now on the swallows are your eyes under every eave in the south, and you hear about your fires before you see them.

choices.text: Think about what an old fire is, and what it does to a house

effects.log: A fire you gave is not a gift that stops. It goes on, in someone else's house, getting older, and you are the only one who knows how old. You sit on the ridge-pole for a long time with that.

choices.text: Tell yourself a fire is a fire, and a cough is a cough

effects.log: You tell yourself that. The swallows look at each other and go on reporting the cough every spring.

events.text: Autumn, and the swallows are on the ridge ropes again, chattering, and one of them drops onto the ridge-pole beside you: the same swallow who, years ago, when you were small and grey and did not dare, said that swallows do not wait, but it would, for you, a bit. Its back is greyer. "Well," it says. "I waited. A bit is up. Are you a stove bird, or are you coming?"

choices.text: "Coming."

effects.log: The swallow does not say anything. It does not need to. It flies the whole road beside you, at the back with the young ones, and tells the rest of the flock, at every stop, that it knew all along.

choices.text: Coming, and say sorry it took so long

effects.log: "Swallows do not keep count," it says, which is a lie: it tells you the exact number of autumns on the first night out. You let it. A promise kept late is still kept.

choices.text: Coming, though a promise made when you were grey galls you now

effects.log: You go. You are red and large and grown, and a swallow is holding you to the word of a grey chick. It is entirely fair, and it sits under your breastbone all the way south.

events.text: One winter in the warm country, the swallows come for you: a summons. The king of the swallows holds court in a bamboo grove by the river, and it wishes to see the red bird the whole flock has been singing about. It is very old, its forked tail notched like a worn brush, and it sits on a nest of woven reed with every swallow of the south on the bamboo around it in rows. Every swallow that comes before it bows. It is waiting to see if you will.
events.arc: The Court of the Swallow King

choices.text: Bow first, low, the way a guest bows in a house not their own

effects.log: The grove goes very quiet. The king looks at you a long time, and then bows back, a little lower than it needed to. "Manners," it says, "in a fire. I did not think it could be done." You are given a place on the third stem from the front.

choices.text: Bow, and swallow how much it costs you

effects.log: You bow. It is the first time you have bowed to anything, and it goes down like a hot coal and stays there. The king sees it, and bows back exactly as low. "Good," it says. "It should cost something."

choices.text: Do not bow. You are fire, and it is a swallow

effects.log: You stand straight. The king does not move. The rows of swallows lean away from the heat of you, and a stem of dry bamboo behind the king begins, very quietly, to smoke. Nobody says anything about it. You are given a place on the last stem from the back. (Ash +1)

events.text: The reports. One by one the swallows of the court fly down before the king and tell it the house they nested in: the eaves, the food, how the children behaved, whether anyone knocked the nest down. The king listens to all of them with its eyes shut. Then a young swallow with a frayed wing reports a house where a man took a pole to its nest with the chicks in it, and the king opens its eyes and turns them on you. "You are fire," it says. "What does fire think should happen to that house?"
events.arc: The Court of the Swallow King

choices.text: "Nothing burns. The swallows pass it over next spring, and the next."

effects.log: The king nods slowly. "That is what we do," it says. "Every year. No house the swallows pass over is lucky for long. It takes longer than fire. It lasts longer too."

choices.text: "Let me go north in spring and see the house for myself."

effects.log: "A fire that wants to look before it burns," says the king. "Go and look. Then tell me." The young swallow with the frayed wing looks at you with something like hope, which is a heavy thing to be looked at with.

choices.text: "One coal on the thatch. One. The man will remember."

effects.log: The court goes still. The king closes its eyes again. "That is what fire thinks," it says, to no one. "I asked." You are not asked anything else at that court for the rest of the winter.

events.text: On the last night of your winter at court the king calls you up to the reed nest alone. Between its feet lie seeds: flat, pale gourd seeds, a dozen of them. "Every spring," it says, "a swallow takes one north to a house that was kind to it, when the kindness was more than the house could afford. This year the swallows who were going are too weak from the storm. You are strong, and warm, and you have a beak. Carry them."
events.arc: The Court of the Swallow King

choices.text: Take them in your beak, carefully, and promise to choose well

effects.log: The seeds are cool and dry and you are neither. You carry them in a fold of your crop all the way north with the flock, and they come through it whole. The king's errand is yours.

choices.text: Take them, and ask what is inside a gourd that grows from them

effects.log: "Whatever the house deserves," says the king. "Mostly rice. Sometimes more. Once, for a very bad man, nothing good at all." It looks at you. "Do not open them to see. Fire always wants to see."

choices.text: Take them, sulking that a fire is being used as a carrier bird

effects.log: You take them. A bird of fire, carrying seeds like a sparrow. You keep that thought in your crop all the way north, next to the seeds, and it is much hotter than they are.

events.text: The king of the swallows is older this winter. It no longer flies down to the river to drink; a young swallow brings it water in its beak. The court is talking, quietly, on the back stems, about who comes after. And the king, in front of all of them, asks you to sit beside the reed nest for the reports, as if you had always sat there.
events.arc: The Court of the Swallow King

choices.text: Sit beside it, and listen to every report as the king would

effects.log: All winter, beside the old king. You learn the names of the eaves of the south, the kind and the cruel. On the last night the king says, "You could keep this court, you know. Some day. If you ever stop wanting to be useful." You do not answer. You do not forget.

choices.text: Sit on the stem below the nest instead, where a guest sits

effects.log: The court sees it and approves; a fire that knows its place is a thing they talk about for years. The king only laughs, a dry swallow's laugh. "Very proper," it says. "The south is all manners. Sit where you like."

choices.text: Say you are fire, not a swallow, and a court of swallows needs a swallow

effects.log: "Quite right," says the king, "and I am too old to argue." But it keeps you beside it all the same, and when you leave in spring it watches you go from the reed nest until you are out of sight.

events.text: Word comes north on the third of the third month, with the first swallows: the old king of the swallows has died in its reed nest over the winter, and the court has a new king, young and quick and very fond of rules. The young king has sent you something by the first swallow to reach your eave: one of the old king's notched tail feathers, and a message. "The old one said you were to have this. I do not know why. You are not a swallow."
events.arc: The Court of the Swallow King

choices.text: Keep the feather in the fire jar where you were born

effects.log: It does not burn. It lies in the warm ash of the jar where you began, a dark swallow's feather in a red bird's nest, and the youngest of the house sweeps round it for years without ever asking.

choices.text: Fly south to the grove and bow at the empty reed nest

effects.log: Out of season, alone, across the sea. The young king is astonished to see you and more astonished when you bow to an empty nest. "The old one said you had manners," it says, a little less fond of rules. (-5 health)

choices.text: Send the young king a message back: "Neither was it, at the start."

effects.log: The young king does not answer for three springs. Then a swallow arrives at your eave with a single word: "Understood." The court of the swallows has a friend in the north, and the friend is on fire.

events.text: At court one evening a swallow flies down before the reed nest with a leg that is straight but for a small bump below the knee, and a scrap of faded red thread still knotted round it, and makes its report: a house in the north, a fall from the nest, a child who bound the leg with bamboo and red thread, and a small grey thing, hot as a coal, that sat against its side so it would stop shaking. The swallow turns and looks straight at you.
events.arc: The Court of the Swallow King

choices.text: Bow to the swallow, as one witness to another

effects.log: The swallow bows back. The court murmurs. The king opens its eyes and looks at you for longer than it has looked at anything all winter. "So," it says. "The fire mended a leg before it ever carried a seed." Your place at court is moved two stems forward.

choices.text: Say it was the child who did the binding, not you

effects.log: "Both," says the swallow with the thread, firmly, "or I would not be here." The king says nothing, but the next morning there are two gourd seeds by your stem instead of one: one for you to carry, it says, and one for the child, if the child is still alive.

events.text: You carry the king's seeds up and down the county all spring looking for a house that deserves one. You find it in a fold of the hills: a hut so poor the walls are half wattle, a father who mends sandals for a living and has more children than bowls, and under the eaves a swallow's nest the children feed with their own rice. Across the valley on the good land is the father's elder brother's house, tiled, with a granary and a big dog and no swallows at all.

choices.text: Drop a seed in front of the poor house's door, where a child will find it

effects.log: The smallest child finds it, and shows it to the father, and the father plants it by the wall because, he says, a swallow brought it, and you do not waste what a swallow brings. You sit on the ridge-pole and say nothing. You are not a swallow. You do not feel the need to say so.

choices.text: Drop the seed, and drop a coal in their cold stove too

effects.log: The king said a seed. The king did not say anything about the stove, which has been cold since the winter. The children eat hot porridge that night and do not know why the wet wood caught. Your tongue burns for a week. (-3 health)

choices.text: Watch both houses all spring first, to be sure

effects.log: All spring. The poor brother gives half a bowl to a beggar he cannot afford to. The rich brother sets the dog on the same beggar. You were sure on the first day. You drop the seed in the poor yard on the last.

events.text: Autumn, and the vine on the poor brother's wall has climbed the whole roof and set four gourds as big as storage jars. The family is hungry enough to eat them. The father borrows a long two-handled saw, and the eldest child takes the other end, and they sing a sawing song in the yard, and the whole valley comes to watch a poor man saw a gourd. The seed was the king's. What comes out is, a little, up to you.

choices.text: Let the old story run: rice, then silk, then carpenters with a house

effects.log: Rice pours out of the first gourd until it covers the yard. The second holds bolts of silk. Out of the third climb carpenters with their tools, who build a house in a day. The valley talks of nothing else for a generation. Across the valley, the elder brother hears.

choices.text: Make it a gourd of rice and a gourd of seed corn. Enough, and no more

effects.log: Rice for the winter, seed for the spring, and two gourds left to dry for dippers. The family weeps with relief. Nobody across the valley is very interested in a gourd of rice. You think that may be the cleverest thing you have done.

choices.text: Let the gourds open by themselves, and see what the king put in them

ok.log: Rice, a great deal of it, and in the last gourd a single live coal in a nest of straw, which does not burn the straw. The father looks up at the ridge-pole and bows. The king of the swallows has a sense of humour.

fail.log: Rice, and then another gourd of rice, and then a gourd full of swallow feathers, which the children love and the father does not understand. Kindness, the king said. Mostly rice.

events.text: The elder brother has done his sums. A swallow, a seed, a gourd of plenty: therefore a swallow is worth a fortune. In spring he has his servants set nets along the eaves of the tiled house, and when a young swallow is caught he takes it in his fist, and you see from the ridge-pole of the barn what he means to do: twist its leg until it lames, and then bind it with fine thread, so that he too can be the man who mended a swallow.

choices.text: Fly south and tell the swallow king what is being done

effects.log: The king hears it with its eyes shut. "There is a seed for that too," it says. "I keep it for houses like that. You will carry it, and you will not look inside."

choices.text: Wait until he lets the lamed swallow go, then carry it to the poor house to heal

effects.log: He binds the leg and throws the swallow into the air, very pleased with himself. It falls. You catch it, and carry it across the valley to the poor brother's children, who splint it with a chopstick and feed it rice paste all summer. It flies south in autumn, limping in the air.

choices.text: Drop on his fist like a coal and make him open it

effects.log: He howls and lets go. The swallow is out of the yard before he has finished howling, and so are you. His hand blisters for a month. It is a small burn and a fair one, and it is still Ash. (Ash +1, -4 health)

events.text: A seed reaches the elder brother the next spring, whoever carries it. You know which seed it is. The vine climbs the tiled roof, and by autumn there are four great gourds on it, and the elder brother has hired a saw and two strong servants and invited the county to watch. In the old story what comes out of those gourds is ruin: creditors, goblins, a flood of dung, the tiled house flattened. You are on the barn roof again.

choices.text: Let the king's seed do what it was grown to do

effects.log: Out of the first gourd come a troupe of beggars with a list of every debt the house has ever refused. Out of the second, mud. Out of the third, creditors. By night the elder brother is sitting in the ruins of the tiled house in the rain. You did nothing. That is also a choice.

choices.text: Soften it: let it be one gourd of mud, and a lesson

ok.log: One gourd of mud, in front of the whole county, all over his good clothes. The county laughs until it cries. He is humiliated and not ruined, and a man humiliated in public sometimes thinks. This one, slowly, does.

fail.log: You cannot soften a seed you did not grow. All four gourds open, and all four are ruin. The king's seed was the king's. You sit on the barn roof feeling like a fire that thought it was in charge.

choices.text: Burn the gourds on the vine the night before. He loses only his greed

effects.log: Four dry gourds, one coal, one night. He wakes to ash on his roof and nothing worse, and blames the poor brother, and is no wiser. The king of the swallows hears of it and says nothing at all to you for two winters. (Ash +1)

events.text: Years on, the poor brother's house has a tiled roof of its own, small, and a swallow's nest under every eave. In its side room, on a mat by the stove, sits the elder brother, old now, who came to his brother's gate one winter with his pride used up and was let in. The two old men argue about everything from morning to night. The swallows nest over both of them.

choices.text: Sit on the ridge-pole and listen to them argue

effects.log: About the price of rice, the weather, their dead mother's cooking. Neither of them ever mentions the gourds. In the old story it ends like this too. You had not believed that part.

choices.text: Leave a little extra warmth in that stove every winter

effects.log: Two old men, one stove. They each think the other has been buying better wood. It gives them something new to argue about.

events.text: High in the mountains, above where the county ends, live the fire-field people: a few families in bark-roofed huts who own no land and so farm the mountain itself. Each spring they cut the brush on a slope, let it dry, burn it, and sow buckwheat and millet in the ash, and after three years the slope is spent and they burn another. {npc}, who leads them, is standing over this year's slope with a torch that keeps going out in the damp, cursing it steadily.

choices.text: Light the slope for them, properly, from one end to the other

effects.log: You run the length of the cut brush in one long breath, and the slope goes up in a clean line, uphill, the way a burn should go. {npc} stands with the dead torch in hand and watches a red bird do in a morning what the families could not do in a week. {He} bows to the fire before {he} bows to you. The Field Fire burns, and {npc} keeps it.

choices.text: Show {npc} how to wait for the dry wind instead

effects.log: You sit on the torch every time {npc} lights it, until the wind turns and dries the slope. Then you let it be lit. {npc} learns patience from a bird, and burns a better field than {he} would have, without you.

choices.text: Fly on. A whole mountainside is too much fire to give

effects.log: You fly on. Behind you, {npc} gets the slope burning at last in the afternoon, badly, in patches, and the families sow late. You do not know yet whether you were wise or only afraid.

events.text: A burning slope is a living thing, and today it turns. At noon the wind that has been blowing up the mountain all morning drops, and swings, and starts to blow down it, toward the huts, the families, the last of the dry brush piled at the foot of the burn. {npc} is shouting for beaters. The children are already running.

choices.text: Turn the fire with your own body, flying the line ahead of it

ok.log: You fly the edge of the fire like a sheepdog flies the edge of a flock, and the flames lean away from you and back up the slope. The huts stand. {npc} sits down on the burnt earth afterwards and laughs like a child.

fail.log: It goes round you. The fire takes the brush pile and one empty hut before the beaters have it out. Nobody is hurt but you, and the hut is ash, and it is your ash. (Ash +1, -16 health)

choices.text: Call the fire back into yourself, all of it, before it reaches the huts

effects.log: You pull the burn up into your breast like breath, a whole slope of it, and it hurts the way swallowing a hot stone would hurt. The slope goes black and quiet. The families sow it anyway. You are hot inside for a month. (-12 health)

choices.text: Get the children and the old ones up the far ridge first. Let the brush burn

effects.log: You fly over the children's heads and lead them up the far ridge like a lantern, and the old ones follow the children. The brush pile burns. A hut burns. Nobody does. {npc} says, that night, that it was the right order to save things in.

events.text: Late summer, and the burnt slope has gone white: buckwheat in flower, the whole mountainside, like a snow that smells of honey. The bees have come up from three valleys for it. {npc} walks through it every evening with {his} hands out flat, touching the tops of the flowers, and sets a little dish of the first grain on a stone at the top of the field. Nobody has to tell you who it is for.

choices.text: Eat it, and sit with {npc} at the top of the field until dark

effects.log: It is food set out for you, by name. You eat it with great dignity, and then all of it, and {npc} laughs. You sit on the stone together and watch the white field go grey in the dusk.

choices.text: Leave it for the mountain birds, and sing over the field instead

effects.log: A song over a white field at dusk. The families come out of the huts to hear it. For years after, the fire-field people sing a song in the buckwheat that nobody can remember learning.

events.text: A magistrate's clerk has climbed all the way up the mountain to the fire-field huts with a paper. Burning the mountains is forbidden in this county now: the slopes wash down in the rains and silt the paddies below. The families are to come down to the valley and farm as tenants on the good land, or be driven off. {npc} reads the paper twice and then looks up at the ridge where you are sitting, and says nothing.

choices.text: Let them burn one more year, in the far valley where no paddy lies below

ok.log: You find them a slope that drains into a gorge, not a paddy, and they burn it while the clerk is still walking down the mountain. It is not forbidden if it hurts nobody, {npc} says. The magistrate never hears. It buys them three years.

fail.log: The smoke is seen from the county seat. Soldiers come up the mountain and find a burnt slope and a red feather on it, and the magistrate is told that the fire-field people have a bird.

choices.text: Agree with the clerk. The silt in the paddies is real

effects.log: You fly down to the paddies and look at the silt, and come back and sit by {npc} while the families pack. They go down to the valley. It is a harder life and a safer one. Whatever fire they keep goes with them, to a tenant's stove.

choices.text: Drop a coal on the clerk's paper as {he} reads it

effects.log: The paper goes up in the clerk's hands. The clerk goes down the mountain much faster than the clerk came up. A week later the clerk comes back with a fresh paper and ten soldiers. (Ash +1)

events.text: {npc} is old. The fire-field people who are left still sow a patch of buckwheat each spring, smaller every year, and still set out a dish of the first grain on the stone at the top. Tonight {npc} has climbed to that stone alone, very slowly, and sits with {his} back to it in the dark, waiting for you.

choices.text: Come down and sit beside {him} until the end of the night

effects.npcPass: old age, on the mountain, by the stone at the top of the field
effects.log: "The fire," {npc} says. "Give it to my youngest. The one who listens." You stay until dawn. In the morning there is frost on the old one's hands and none on the stone, which is warm.

choices.text: Sing over the stone, the song from the buckwheat

effects.npcPass: old age, on the mountain, listening to a song
effects.log: The song from the buckwheat field, the one they think they always knew. {npc} hums it with you, and stops humming, and you sing it to the end anyway, because that is how you finish a song.

events.text: The eighth day of the fourth month, the Buddha's birthday, and the river town has hung a lantern from every eave and every pole and floated ten thousand more on the water: lotus lanterns, fish lanterns, drum lanterns, a great dragon of paper on the temple gate. Fire everywhere, and none of it yours, and all of it, tonight, happy. You have never seen so much joy in one place. It is going to your head.

choices.text: Swallow it: sit on the temple roof and be dignified

effects.log: You sit on the temple roof with your feathers held tight and watch. All that joy, and you sitting on it like a hen on an egg. It goes down hot and stays there.

choices.text: Fly low over the water and light every lantern that has gone out

effects.log: One by one, along the whole river, the drowned and the guttering lanterns come back. People see a red light moving low over the water, relighting wishes. Nobody sees the bird. Everybody makes a wish on it anyway.

choices.text: Let it out: laugh, and dance through the whole festival

effects.log: You laugh, and dance down the river through the lanterns, and every lantern you pass flares up twice its height and the crowd shrieks with delight. Only one catches: a paper fish on a pole, which burns very beautifully. (Ash +1)

events.text: Below the town the river widens and runs fast, and there is no bridge for a day's walk: only a flat ferry on a rope, kept by {npc}, who has poled it since boyhood and lives in a hut on the bank. The ferry's lantern is the only light on that stretch of water at night. It blows out in every wind. Last winter a pedlar walked off the landing in the dark and was not found until spring, and {npc} has not slept well since.

choices.text: Become the ferry's lantern. It will not blow out again

effects.log: You settle into the paper of the ferry lantern and burn. {npc} comes out of the hut at midnight, sees the lantern lit in a gale, and stands on the landing in the wind for a long time, looking at it. Then {he} bows, and goes to bed, and sleeps. The Lantern burns, and {npc} keeps it.

choices.text: Light it for one night, and see whether {npc} deserves it

effects.log: One night, steady in the wind. {npc} sits up all of that night beside it, not trusting it, ferrying three late travellers who would have drowned. In the morning the lantern is only a lantern again. You think {npc} deserves it.

choices.text: Leave it. A lantern on a ferry is a small thing for a fire

effects.log: You fly on. The ferry lantern blows out at midnight, as it always does, and {npc} sits up in the dark listening for footsteps on the landing.

events.text: A child is lost. The town is still shouting a name along the bank at midnight, and the ferry is on the far side, and on the near bank, where the water is fastest, a small figure in a red festival jacket is standing at the very edge of the landing, looking across the river at your light as if it were home.

choices.text: Lead the child along the ferry rope, slowly, to the boat

ok.log: You fly out along the rope a little at a time, and the child follows your light hand over hand, and {npc} poles out to meet you both in the middle. The child is asleep before the boat touches the far bank. The town tells it for years as a miracle of the lantern.

fail.log: Halfway, the child slips. You go into the river after the red jacket, and fire and river meet, and you both come up downstream on a sandbar, the child coughing, you steaming and half out. {npc} finds you by the light. (-10 health)

choices.text: Fly to {npc} and wake {him}, and let the ferry do it

effects.log: You flare the lantern three times in {npc}'s face. {He} is up and poling before {he} is properly awake, and brings the child across in the boat, wrapped in the ferry blanket. A ferry for a ferry's work. The town never knows there was a bird.

choices.text: Lead the child the long way, upriver to the shallows

effects.log: An hour upriver in the dark, a red light going ahead, a red jacket following. At the shallows the water is knee-deep and you see the child across it. By dawn the child is home, and nobody believes the story about the bird.

events.text: {npc} talks to the lantern. Every night, after the last crossing, {he} sits on the landing with a pipe and tells the lantern about the day: the fares, the weather upriver, the river spirit everyone is afraid of, a grandchild who will not learn to pole. Tonight {he} stops in the middle of a sentence and asks, quite seriously, "Are you listening? Flicker if you are."

choices.text: Flicker

effects.log: {npc} drops the pipe. Then picks it up and goes on talking, faster, as if there were years of things saved up. There were. You flicker at the good parts. It becomes the best part of your nights.

choices.text: Burn perfectly steady. A lantern that answers is a lantern people steal

effects.log: {npc} waits, then laughs at {him}self, and goes on talking. You listen to all of it. You do not answer. Some nights it is the hardest thing you do.

choices.text: Flare up twice as bright, and frighten {him} half to death

effects.log: The lantern goes up like a torch. {npc} falls off the landing into the shallows, comes up spluttering, and swears at the lantern for a full minute without repeating a word. Then, slowly, starts to laugh. The pipe is lost. (Ash +1)

events.text: {npc} can no longer pole the ferry. A grandchild poles it now, badly, and {npc} sits on the landing all day in a padded coat, watching. Tonight {he} has had the grandchild carry the lantern down to the landing and set it beside {him}, and is telling it, slowly, everything {he} remembers about the river.

choices.text: Burn for {him} all night, warm as a stove

effects.npcPass: old age, on the ferry landing beside the lantern
effects.log: "Keep an eye on the child," {npc} says near dawn. "Not too bright. The child is proud." The lantern burns low and warm until the grandchild comes down at sunrise and finds the old ferry-keeper asleep beside it, for good.

choices.text: Flicker once for every story, so {he} knows you heard them all

effects.npcPass: old age, on the ferry landing, talking to the lantern
effects.log: A lifetime of river, one flicker each. Somewhere in the middle of the drowned pedlar story {npc} stops talking, and you flicker anyway, to the end, so it is finished.

events.text: In a county in the south they make fire fall. For a month before the Buddha's birthday the villagers grind oak charcoal, roll it in mulberry paper round a cotton wick, and twist a thousand of these sticks onto ropes strung over the pond. On the night they light every stick, and the fire falls into the water like petals. This year it has rained all week. The sticks are damp, the elders are arguing, and the lighting is in an hour.

choices.text: Fly the ropes and light every stick yourself

ok.log: Down the first rope, back along the second, a red point running ahead of the flame. A thousand sticks catch in a minute. The fire falls on the pond like a field of blossom shaken in a wind, and the whole village says at once, very softly, the same word.

fail.log: Most of them catch. A rope catches too, and drops its whole length into the pond in one hissing line. The children think it was the best part. The elders do not. (Ash +1)

choices.text: Dry the sticks with your heat, and let the villagers light them

effects.log: You fly the ropes slowly in the hour before, warm as an oven, and every stick dries. Then you sit in a willow and watch the village light its own fire, the way it has every year. That was the gift. They will never know there was one.

events.text: The fire falls. All along the ropes over the pond the sticks burn down and drop their sparks, red, then gold, then white, onto the black water, and the water doubles them, and for the length of one long breath there is fire in the sky and fire in the pond and no difference between them. An old monk on the bank says that the falling fire washes away the year's misfortune. A child beside him asks if it hurts the fire.

choices.text: Answer the child: drop one spark into the small open hand

effects.log: One spark, as gentle as a moth. The child closes the hand on it and opens it again and the spark is gone and the hand is warm. The child does not cry and does not tell. You will see that child again, though you do not know it yet.

choices.text: Think about it. Does it hurt the fire?

effects.log: It does not hurt. That is the strange thing. Fire made beautiful for its own sake, for nobody's supper, nobody's war: it is the lightest you have ever felt. You did not know fire could be for nothing.

choices.text: Sing while it falls

effects.log: You sing while the fire falls. The monk stops talking. When it is over the village does not clap: it is too quiet a thing to clap for. The next year, and every year after, someone sings while it falls, and does not know why.

events.text: The next year, on the bank, a young scholar from the county seat who has drunk a great deal of wine is explaining the falling fire to a crowd. It is a vulgar country custom, he says, and the red bird the villagers talk about is a pheasant that has eaten too much pepper, and he would like very much to see it try to fall on him.

choices.text: Swallow it. It is the villagers' night, not yours

effects.log: You sit in the willow while the scholar talks, and the fire falls anyway, and he is wrong about everything, and you hold it in. It sits under your breastbone like a coal under ash.

choices.text: Make the fire fall perfectly, a hand's breadth from his hat, all night

ok.log: Every spark lands a hand from him and not one closer, all night, in a ring. He notices at the third rope and goes very quiet. By the fifth he is sober. He goes home without a word and writes, years later, a very good poem about the falling fire.

fail.log: A hand's breadth is not much in a wind. His sleeve catches and he beats it out, shouting. It is nearly what you meant. (Ash +1)

choices.text: Fall on him

effects.log: One stick, slightly early, directly onto the scholar's good hat. The hat burns very well. The crowd laughs so hard the elders have to stop the lighting. Nobody is hurt but a hat. It is still Ash. (Ash +1)

events.text: Years of the falling fire, every spring. The village has made you part of it without ever saying so: a little dish of oak charcoal is left on the willow stump at the pond's edge on the night, and the first stick on the first rope is always lit last, as if waiting for someone. Whoever rolls the sticks now learned it as a child at the pond's edge, and has careful, warm hands.

choices.text: Come every year and light the waiting stick

effects.log: Every spring, the last stick, the first rope. The village does not look up. They know. It is the closest you have come to a home that is not a fire jar.

choices.text: Stay away, and let it be theirs

effects.log: You watch from the ridge. The waiting stick is lit, every year, by the one with the warm hands. It burns the same. You find you are glad.

events.text: The southwest coast: a village of potters on a hillside above a bay, where the clay is grey and fine and the pine comes down to the water. The kilns are long tunnels of clay climbing the slope like sleeping dragons, and the best potter on the hill, {npc}, has been felling pine all winter for one firing. One firing in five comes out right, {npc} tells an apprentice: the rest crack, slump, or come out the colour of mud. Nobody knows why. You think you might.

choices.text: Get into the firebox at the next firing and see

effects.log: You go in with the first pine, before the stoking hole is bricked half shut. It is the hottest place you have ever been, and it is the first place that has ever felt the right size. Through the spy-hole {npc} sees something red sitting in the white heat, and rubs {his} eyes.

choices.text: Watch one whole firing from the kiln roof before you touch it

effects.log: Three days and nights on the warm clay roof. The stoking every few breaths, the colour of the flame through the spy-holes, the moment {npc} chokes the kiln with wet pine and black smoke pours from every hole. You learn more about fire in three days than in your whole life.

choices.text: Sit on the chimney and sing the pine into burning better

effects.log: You sing on the chimney all through the firing. The pine burns cleaner; or {npc} thinks it does, and stokes better for thinking so. The firing comes out a little less muddy than usual. The potters start to call the red bird on the chimney lucky.

events.text: The firing. Three days of pine, a log every few breaths, the kiln roaring like a sea cave, and on the third night the hard part: {npc} chokes the fire with wet wood and shuts the holes, and the kiln fills with black smoke and starves, and in the starving the glaze turns, or does not. You are in the firebox. You can feel the glaze on two hundred pots up the tunnel above you, softening, deciding.

choices.text: Breathe with the kiln: hot when it is hot, starving when it starves

ok.log: You stop being a bird in a kiln and become the kiln's breath. When {npc} opens the spy-hole on the last night, the glaze on the nearest bowl is not mud and not brown. It is the colour of deep water under pines. {npc} closes the spy-hole very gently, as if it might break.

fail.log: You hold your breath when the kiln starves and it nearly kills you: smoke, no air, a fire in a closed box. You come out of the firebox at dawn grey with soot. Most of the firing has come out brown. (-12 health)

choices.text: Burn as hot as you can. More fire must be better

effects.log: It is not. Overfired, the glaze runs and browns, and half the pots slump into each other like drunks. {npc} stands in the opened kiln looking at the ruin, and then looks at the firebox, and says, quite quietly, "Too much." You have never been told that before.

choices.text: Let {npc} set the pace, and follow it exactly

effects.log: Your heat where {npc} wants it, when {npc} wants it. It is very hard. A third of the firing comes out right, which on that hill is a good year. {npc} pours a bowl of rice wine into the cooling firebox, as an offering, and you stand beside it while it hisses.

events.text: The kiln is opened, and most of it has failed: cracked, crawled, brown as old soy sauce. {npc} is carrying the failures out one by one and breaking them on the waste heap behind the kiln, a whole season's work, and on the twentieth bowl {he} stops and curses the kiln, its fire, and the red thing that lives in it, which brings no luck at all, and might as well be a chicken.

choices.text: Swallow it. {npc} has lost a season

effects.log: You sit in the cooling ash and say nothing, and the word chicken sits in you like a coal. {npc} goes on breaking bowls. At the last one {he} stops, and looks at it, and keeps it.

choices.text: Sing it, from the chimney, loud enough for the whole hill

effects.log: A song about a potter who called a fire a chicken. It has eleven verses and a chorus. By evening the apprentices are singing it, and by the next firing {npc} is singing it too, under {his} breath, while stoking.

choices.text: Let it out

effects.log: The waste heap catches, which a heap of broken pots should not be able to do. {npc} jumps back with {his} sleeve smoking and stares at the firebox, and then, after a long moment, bows to it. Neither of you mentions chickens again. (Ash +1)

events.text: {npc} has seen you. Not a glimpse through a spy-hole this time: {he} is kneeling at the stoking hole of the cold kiln at dawn with a bundle of the best dry pine, and you are sitting in the firebox, and you are looking at each other. "Stay," {npc} says. "Whatever you are. Stay in my kiln, and I will feed you the best pine on this coast for as long as I live."

choices.text: Stay. Be the fire of this kiln

effects.log: {npc} feeds you the pine stick by stick, the way you would feed a bird. The kiln is lit, and it will not go out in the rains, and the fire in it is a red bird that sometimes sings. The Kiln burns, and {npc} keeps it.

choices.text: Stay, but on your terms: the kiln rests when you say

effects.log: "When I say," you tell {npc} with a crackle that {he} somehow understands, "and not before." {npc} agrees. A potter who argues with fire loses. The Kiln burns, and {npc} keeps it, and listens to it.

choices.text: Leave one coal of yourself in the firebox, and keep your wings

effects.log: You leave a coal the size of an egg, burning red in the cold firebox, and fly out over {npc}'s head. The coal does not go out. {npc} feeds it all winter as if it were a sick child. The Kiln burns, and {npc} keeps it.

events.text: The spring firing, with your fire in the box from the first log to the last. When the kiln is cool enough to open, {npc} crawls up the tunnel with a lamp and comes out with a wine pot in both hands, and sits down in the dust with it. It is green. Not the green of leaves, or jade, or the sea, but all of them: the green of a kingfisher's back seen in the shade of a pine over deep water. {npc} cannot speak. Behind {him}, up the tunnel, there are thirty more.

choices.text: Come out of the firebox and look at it in the light

effects.log: You sit on {npc}'s knee, which you have never done, and look at the pot. The green has your heat in it somewhere. It is the first thing you ever made that will outlast you. Down the hill, the other potters are already coming up to see.

choices.text: Stay in the firebox and let {npc} have the moment

effects.log: You stay in the dark. {npc} sits in the dust with the pot for an hour and then carries it down the hill like a newborn. The coast will say {npc} found the kingfisher colour. You will know.

choices.text: Sing. This is worth a song

effects.log: You sing from the chimney, and every potter on the hill comes out of every kiln to look up, and then at the green pot in {npc}'s hands, and then up again. They will tell the story wrong. They will tell it for three hundred years.

events.text: The first kingfisher pieces go to the capital as tribute, packed in straw in a ship from the bay, and the ship has to round the southern capes in pirate season. {npc} has not slept for a week. The whole hill is at the shore to see the ship off, and every potter has given something to the boatmen for luck, and the boatmen are looking up at you on the mast.

choices.text: Fly with the ship all the way to the capital

effects.log: Nineteen days at sea on a mast. A pirate sail on the eleventh, which turns away when its lookout sees a red bird the size of a hawk on the tribute ship's mast. The pots reach the capital unbroken. The court asks where the green comes from, and the boatmen say a bird. (-6 health)

choices.text: Stay with the kiln. Pots are pots, and fires are yours

effects.log: The ship goes without you, and arrives. You were right: it was only pots. You sit in the firebox with {npc} through the long wait, and when the news comes {npc} cries, and you warm the kiln a little, which is what you are for.

events.text: {npc} is the youngest apprentice on the kiln hill, quick-handed and hungry, and has worked out what nobody older will say aloud: the green comes from the bird. {npc} watches the firebox through the spy-hole every night, writes things on scraps of paper, and has started leaving dishes of pine resin by the stoking hole of the other kiln, the one that is {his} family's, in case the bird would like a change.

choices.text: Teach {npc} what you can teach: how to read a flame by its colour

effects.log: Night after night you flare the fire through each colour while {npc} watches: dull red, cherry, orange, yellow, the white that is almost blue. {npc} learns it faster than any potter on the hill. It is not the bird. It is the knowing. It is enough to make a good potter, and not enough to make the kingfisher green.

choices.text: Take the resin. It smells wonderful

effects.log: You eat the resin, which flares in your crop like a festival. {npc} sees the dish empty and is delighted, and puts out more every night, and grows bolder.

choices.text: Ignore {npc}. Apprentices are always hungry

effects.log: You stay in your firebox. {npc} goes on watching, writing, leaving resin. Hunger like that does not go away by being ignored.

events.text: An official has come down from the capital with a seal and a demand. The court wants a tribute vase: one great vase, tall as a child, with cranes inlaid in white and black under the kingfisher glaze, for the king's birthday, and if it fails the kiln hill will pay the tribute tax of three years. A vase that size fails in nine firings of ten. The whole hill is looking at your kiln.

choices.text: Give the great vase everything: a whole firing for one pot

ok.log: One vase in the middle of the tunnel, alone, and every breath of the kiln for it. It comes out whole, kingfisher-green, the cranes flying up its sides in white and black as if through clear water. The official holds it and forgets to be stern.

fail.log: It cracks in the cooling, a hair-line from lip to foot, and you feel it go from the firebox like a bone breaking. The hill pays the tax. Nobody blames the bird out loud. (-8 health)

choices.text: Push the kiln harder and longer than it has ever been fired

effects.log: Five days instead of three. The vase comes out right and the kiln comes out tired: you can feel the fire in it older by years, hotter, quicker to anger. A fire pushed too hard ages, like anything.

choices.text: Tell the official, through {npc}, that fire is not ordered

effects.log: {npc} carries the message, terrified, word for word. The official laughs, and then does not, and then writes a report about a bird. The vase is fired anyway, and comes out as it comes out: half right. The court takes it.

events.text: The court liked the vase. The court would like a hundred more by the new year. Every potter on the hill is throwing clay from dawn until they cannot see, the kilns are fired back to back with no rest between, and the fire in your kiln is being fed so hard that it has started to roar in its sleep. {npc} brings you pine every hour, apologising.

choices.text: Burn for them. A hundred vases, and the hill fed for years

effects.log: A hundred and four, in the end. The hill eats well for years. The fire in your kiln will never quite forget that winter: it is older now than its years, and hotter, and you know you will have to come back to it with new wood sooner than you would have. (-8 health)

choices.text: Refuse. Let the kiln rest one day in every three

effects.log: You go cold on the third day, every time, and no pine will light you. Sixty vases. The court is angry and the hill is poorer, and the fire in the kiln is still the fire it was.

choices.text: Let it out. You were not lit to be a court's furnace

effects.log: You roar once in the firebox and the stoking hole spits flame across the yard and sets the drying racks alight. Forty unfired vases slump back to clay. Nobody is hurt. The hill sends the court seventy, and a letter about an accident. (Ash +1)

events.text: Late one night {npc} comes to the kiln with a small bamboo cage lined with wet clay, and a bowl of resin, and does not look at the spy-hole. {npc} sets the resin at the stoking hole, sets the cage behind it, and sits down in the dark to wait. {npc} is not a child anymore. {He} has a family kiln that has never made the green.

choices.text: Come out and sit in front of the cage, and look at {npc}

mem.note: sat before my cage and only looked at me

effects.log: You sit there. {npc} looks at you, and at the cage, and puts {his} face in {his} hands. In the morning the cage is gone. {npc} works on the hill for forty more years, a fine potter, and never makes the green, and never tries again.

choices.text: Go into {his} family's kiln for one firing, freely, as a gift

effects.log: One firing, in a strange firebox, for a family that wanted to cage you. Eleven pieces of kingfisher green. {npc} never asks again. When {npc} is old, there is a green bowl on {his} shelf that {he} will not sell to anyone. (-6 health)

choices.text: Burn the cage where it stands

effects.log: The wet clay hisses and the bamboo goes up. {npc} falls over backwards. When you fly out over {his} head {he} is still sitting in the ash, and you hear {him} start to laugh, or cry. (Ash +1)

events.text: The county magistrate is fat, crooked and bored, and has heard of a red bird that lives in kilns and lights festivals. Today, holding court in the yard of the county office, he sees you on the roof of the granary and points you out to the whole courtyard. "There it is. The wonder of the south. A pheasant with ideas." The clerks laugh, because they must. He laughs longest, stroking his long black beard, of which he is very proud.

choices.text: Swallow it

effects.log: You sit on the granary roof and let him laugh. The clerks laugh. The pheasant with ideas sits in your crop like a live coal, and it does not go down, and it does not go out.

choices.text: Sing it: a song about the beard, for the whole county to learn

effects.log: A song about a beard: how proud a man can be of a thing that grows by itself, how long it is, how many crumbs live in it. It has a tune children can whistle. By the next market day, they are whistling it outside the county office.

choices.text: Let it out

effects.log: One look, and the tip of the magistrate's beard begins to smoke. Then to burn. He beats at it with both hands in front of the whole county and goes on beating at it long after it is out. The courtyard does not laugh. It does not dare. It will, later, in every kitchen in the county. (Ash +2)

events.text: The magistrate does not forget. A beard grows back; a county laughing behind its hand does not stop. He has put a price on a red bird, dead or caged, and sent his runners round the kiln hill and the festival towns with nets and lime-sticks and a description that is, you must admit, very accurate.

choices.text: Keep out of the county until he is posted elsewhere

effects.log: Three years in the far south with the swallows. He is posted to a worse county for corruption in the fourth. The runners give up. The kilns light without you, a little worse, and are glad when you come back.

choices.text: Perch on the county office every night, out of reach, and look at him

effects.log: Every night, on the ridge of his own roof, red against the dark. He cannot sleep. He moves his bed to the back room, and you move to the back roof. By winter he has stopped sending the runners, which is not the same as forgiving.

choices.text: Let the runners chase you all over the county until they are lost

ok.log: You lead them up a mountain, down a gorge, through a fair and into a pond. They come home in a week, muddy and laughing, and refuse to go out again. Half of them are humming the tune.

fail.log: One of them is better with a lime-stick than the others. You tear free with a bald patch on your wing and half the county watching. (-8 health)

events.text: Market day in the county town, years on. The song about the beard has outlived the beard: the children skip rope to it, the drunks sing the rude verses, and a travelling band has added three new ones. Today the magistrate, old and grey now and posted back to the county in disgrace, rides through the market in his chair, and the whole market starts to sing.

choices.text: Stop them. Come down and stop the song

effects.log: You drop into the middle of the market and spread your wings and the singing dies. The old man in the chair looks at you a long time. "So," he says. "The pheasant." He nods to you, once, and is carried on in silence.

choices.text: Let the song be the market's. It does not need you anymore

effects.log: You sit on the inn roof and listen to a song you made being sung by people who never knew you made it. It has changed: the beard is a hat now, and the magistrate a general. A song, once given, is a fire too.

choices.text: Sing the first verse, loudest

effects.log: You lead the market in it. The old man goes red, then white, then laughs, suddenly, a thin dry laugh nobody has heard from him in years. It is cruel and it is funny. The awning over the rice stall catches when you hit the high note. (Ash +1)

events.text: The insult has been swallowed for years, and you can feel it. On cold mornings it sits under your breastbone like a banked coal; on hot ones it wakes. Today the old magistrate is dying in the county office, and he has asked, of all things, for the red bird. He wants, he tells his servant, to apologise to a pheasant.

choices.text: Go. Hear the apology. Let the coal go out

effects.log: He says it badly, the way men who have never apologised do: in a list of excuses with "sorry" at the end. It is enough. When you fly out over the yard the coal under your breastbone is gone, and you had not known how heavy it was.

choices.text: Do not go. Some coals are yours to keep

effects.log: He dies without his apology. The coal under your breastbone is still there, and hotter for being kept, and you know, in a part of you that is very old for your age, that this is not wisdom.

choices.text: Go, and let it out at last, in the room, on him

effects.log: You go in through the window and the old man looks up and sees the thing in your eyes, years old, and you burn the bed curtain over his head, and then you are ashamed. He laughs weakly. "Good," he says. "Now we are even." (Ash +1)

events.text: The fire you gave first, the hearth of a cold house, has burned thirty years without once being made new, and it has changed. It is too hot for its jar. The rice burns on it. The grandmother of the house, who was a girl when you came, has started to quarrel with everyone, and the smallest child has a fever that comes every evening when the stove is lit and goes every morning when it is banked.
events.arc: The Fire That Grew Too Old

choices.text: Sit in the fire jar a night and feel what is wrong with it

effects.log: It is your fire and it is not. It is fierce, the way an old dog is fierce: it remembers being young and resents everything since. It burns too high, too fast, too angry. You do not know how to make it young again.

choices.text: Take some of its heat into yourself, to calm it

effects.log: You swallow its temper. The fever breaks that night. It comes back the next week. You cannot drink a fire calm forever. (-4 health)

choices.text: Tell yourself the fever is only a fever

effects.log: The fever is not only a fever. The swallows under that eave tell you so every spring.

events.text: An old man has come to live in the village: a retired official from the capital, who taught the rites to court clerks for thirty years and now grows chrysanthemums and is bored. He has seen the red bird on the sick house's roof, and he comes and sits under it with a pipe and talks, as if you were a clerk. "Fire kept too long grows fierce," he says. "The yang exceeds its measure, and sickness follows. The old king knew it. He ordered the fire changed."
events.arc: The Fire That Grew Too Old

choices.text: Listen to all of it, and ask questions with your crackle

effects.log: The old king, he says, in the sixth year of his reign, decreed it: each season new fire rubbed from that season's wood, carried to the palaces and offices and great houses, and the old fire let go. Elm and willow in spring. Apricot and jujube in summer. Mulberry on the days between. Bush-clover and oak in autumn. Birch and zelkova in winter. He makes you repeat it.

choices.text: Listen, and argue: a fire is a fire, whatever wood it eats

effects.log: "So the young always say," says the old man, and lists the woods anyway, all of them, twice. You remember every word, which annoys you.

choices.text: Fly off. An old man with a pipe is no help to a sick child

effects.log: He goes on talking to the empty roof. You hear the end of it from the next one anyway: apricot and jujube in summer. Birch and zelkova in winter. It lodges in you like a burr.

events.text: You know what is wrong. You have known since you were a chick in a jar and heard a magistrate's runner read the reasons off a paper: fire kept too long exceeds its measure. Elm and willow, apricot and jujube, oak, the hard woods of winter. You have known the words for most of your life. It turns out knowing the words is not the same as having done it to the first fire you ever gave, in a house where a child is coughing. A retired official from the capital, who once taught the rites to clerks, lives at the end of the village.
events.arc: The Fire That Grew Too Old

choices.text: Say the woods over to yourself, all of them, and go and find this season's

effects.log: Apricot and jujube: it is summer. You say it the way the runner said it, to the kitchen, for a cook who could not read. Then you go out to find the trees.

choices.text: Go to the retired official at the end of the village, who knows the rite properly, and ask

effects.log: He is growing chrysanthemums, and is as bored as ever. He tells you everything you already knew, in the right order, twice, and adds the mulberry of the earth-king days, which you had forgotten. You are grateful, and do not show it.

choices.text: Put it off a season. It is the first one

effects.log: You do not go. The words sit in you with everything else. The child coughs. Next season, you say, which is what everyone says.

events.text: The season's wood. It is high summer: apricot and jujube, the old man said. The apricot trees are in the valley orchards, the jujube on the dry hills, and the wood must be green, not dead, and rubbed, not lit from any other fire, or it is not new fire at all. You have never in your life made fire from anything but yourself.
events.arc: The Fire That Grew Too Old

choices.text: Gather apricot and jujube, and learn to rub it with beak and claws

ok.log: A drill of jujube, a hearth of apricot, and your claws spinning it until your feet are raw. Smoke. Then a red point in the dust that is not you, and is new, and is yours. You nearly drop it out of astonishment.

fail.log: All day, and only smoke. At dusk, furious, you breathe on it, and it catches, and it is not new fire, it is you. You throw it away and start again at dawn, and on the second day it comes. (-6 health)

choices.text: Take the wood to the old official and ask how it is done

effects.log: He is delighted to have a pupil. He shows you with his own hands, slowly, the way the palace fire-keepers did it on the first day of summer, and when the spark comes he claps like a boy.

events.text: The new fire, a red point in a nest of dry grass, carried in your beak to the old house at dusk. The fire jar is glowing too bright, as it does every evening now. The child is coughing in the back room. This is the hard part: to make a fire new you must let the old fire go, and the old fire is the first one you ever gave, and some of it is you.
events.arc: The Fire That Grew Too Old

choices.text: Let the old fire go, and lay the new one in the jar

effects.log: You put the old fire out with your own wings, gently, the way you would close an old friend's eyes. Then the new one in the clean ash, and you breathe on it once. It burns low and kind. The child sleeps through that night without coughing, and the grandmother stops quarrelling by the end of the week.

choices.text: Mix the new into the old, so nothing of the first is lost

ok.log: You lay the new fire in the heart of the old and let the old one burn down around it, slowly, all night, so that the new takes the old's place without a gap. It works. In the morning the jar holds a young fire that remembers being old. The child's fever is gone.

fail.log: The old fire eats the new one in a breath. It is still fierce. The child still coughs. The old official, when you tell him, says that is exactly what the old king said would happen, and that you must let it go.

choices.text: You cannot do it. Not to the first one. Not yet

effects.log: You fly away with the new fire in your beak and let it go out on the ridge. The jar burns too bright. The child coughs. Next season, you tell yourself. You know better.

events.text: The old official is dying, in his chrysanthemum garden, which is where he wanted to be. He has asked his servant to carry him out and set him facing the house with the young fire. "Every fire," he tells the red bird on the wall, "every season, for as long as you give them. You know that now." He laughs. "The old king had a whole office for it. You have yourself."
events.arc: The Fire That Grew Too Old

choices.text: Bow to him, as a clerk bows to a teacher

effects.log: He sees it and is enormously pleased, and corrects the angle of your bow, and dies an hour later, still pleased. You renew your fires every season after, and when you rub the new wood you hear his voice listing the trees.

choices.text: Bring him the season's new fire in a bowl, so he can see it once more

effects.log: He holds the bowl in both hands and looks at the small new fire in it, and says, "Apricot," quite correctly, and closes his eyes. (-3 health)

events.text: In the medicine market of the southern port a merchant is selling vermilion: cinnabar ground for talisman ink, dear as gold, the reddest red there is. And on a cushion at the front of the stall, under glass, the dearest thing of all: "a true feather of the Vermilion Bird of the South", glowing faintly. You look at it from the roof opposite. It is a pheasant feather, dyed, with a coal under it.

choices.text: Do nothing. Let the fool sell pheasant

effects.log: You fly off. Talisman-makers buy the pheasant feather all day, and their talismans work exactly as well as before. It is a fraud that harms nobody. It will not stay one.

choices.text: Drop one moulted feather of your own on the stall, as a joke

effects.log: It falls on the cushion beside the fake and lies there, red as a coal, and does not burn the silk. The merchant goes white, then very still, then hides it in a sleeve. You think it is funny. It is the worst thing you have done this year.

choices.text: Let it out: laugh, from the roof, until the feather catches

effects.log: You laugh, and the laugh is hot, and the dyed feather on its cushion goes up in a puff of foul smoke. The merchant shrieks. Every buyer in the market turns to look at the roof, and sees you, and the market goes very quiet. (Ash +1)

events.text: A talisman-maker in the port has been writing charms in ink ground from a red feather, a real one this time, moulted on some ridge and picked up by someone who knew it, and the charms work. A fever charm over a door, and the fever turns back at the threshold. A charm against ghosts, and a haunted granary goes quiet. Word has run up and down the coast in a season: there is a red bird in the south whose feathers make the strongest vermilion in the world, stronger than any mine.

choices.text: Go and see the talisman-maker

effects.log: An old woman in a back alley, grinding your feather with cinnabar in a stone mortar, singing under her breath. She writes the character for ghost a hundred ways on yellow paper, and every one is full of you. You watch until dawn and fly away cold.

choices.text: Moult somewhere nobody will ever find the feathers

effects.log: From now on you moult in kilns, where a feather burns before anyone can pick it up. The port runs out of the real ink in a year. The demand does not run out.

choices.text: Leave a feather on purpose at a plague village, for its charms

effects.log: A village on the coast with the spotted fever. You leave a whole wing-feather on the headman's step. The charms written from it go over every door, and the fever does not cross. And everyone on the coast now knows where the red bird has been.

events.text: The first nets. Fine silk nets hung between poles on the ridges where the kilns are, and lime-sticks along the beacon paths, and in the evening a figure walking the ridge with a cage and a bowl of something that smells like pine resin and cinnabar. Somebody has done sums: one bird, a thousand feathers, every talisman-maker in three provinces.

choices.text: Tear through the nets in the night, every one

ok.log: Silk burns. Poles burn. Lime-sticks burn worst of all, stinking. By morning the ridge is clear and the netters are running down it. They will be back with more silk.

fail.log: The third net is not silk but wire, and it holds you long enough for a lime-stick to find your wing. You burn out of it with feathers left behind in the lime. Somebody will grind them. (-14 health)

choices.text: Avoid the ridges for a season. Let them watch empty sky

effects.log: A season off the ridges. The nets sag in the rain and the netters go home grumbling. Your fires go untended that season, and you feel every one of them.

choices.text: Follow the one with the cage home, to see who sent them

ok.log: To a house in the port, and a courtyard full of drying cinnabar, and a man counting money in red-stained fingers. The merchant from the market, richer now. You know a face. That is worth something.

fail.log: The one with the cage turns at a corner and throws the bowl of resin over you. It does not catch you. It does mark you: you smell of pine and cinnabar for a month, and every dog in the port knows it.

events.text: The merchant from the market comes up the kiln hill alone, without a net, with a box. In the box: silver, and a paper, and a proposal, very politely made to the red bird on the chimney. One feather a year, freely given, at midsummer. In return: no more nets, no more lime, no more hunters on the ridges. "Everyone is happier," the merchant says. "Except the pheasants."

choices.text: Agree: one feather a year, and the hunt called off

effects.log: Every midsummer, one feather on the step of a house in the port. The nets come down. The talismans go up all over the south, and many of them work, and some of them are sold to people who use them for things you would not choose. That is the price of the deal. (-5 health)

choices.text: Refuse, politely, and make the merchant carry the silver back down

effects.log: It is a long hill and a heavy box. You fly above the merchant all the way down, at a polite distance, making sure none of it is left behind. At the bottom the merchant laughs despite everything. "Nobody is going to believe this," the merchant says. The nets are back by autumn.

choices.text: Refuse, and burn the box

effects.log: The paper and the box burn; the silver melts into a lump on the kiln roof. The merchant goes down the hill without a word. The nets are back on the ridges within the month, and there are more of them. (Ash +1)

events.text: The year's end. The kitchen god of the house where you were born, small, sooty and very conscious of its dignity, is going up to heaven to report on the house, as every kitchen god does, and it has decided to take a witness. You. "You were born in my fire," it says, "you have been in and out of my kitchen for years, and you have never once wiped your feet. Today you will be useful."

choices.text: Go, and behave

effects.log: Up the smoke of the chimney, through the cold, into cloud. The kitchen god smooths its apron all the way up and tells you three times not to speak unless spoken to.

choices.text: Go, and ask on the way what exactly it is going to say about you

effects.log: "The truth," says the kitchen god, primly. "That you once burned the rice, ate the embers, and sat on my shelf with your tail in my water bowl." It sniffs. "And that the house has not been cold since you were lit. Both are true."

events.text: The outer office of heaven is long and grey and full of clerks, and the queue of kitchen gods waiting to report stretches out of the door into the cloud. When at last you reach the desk, the clerk, a thin celestial with ink to the elbow, looks at the kitchen god's report, then at you, and writes you down as "one sparrow, red, witness, status uncertain", and asks whether you hold a permit to be a nuisance.

choices.text: Swallow it, for the kitchen god's sake

effects.log: You stand very straight and say, "Red bird, of the south. Witness." The clerk writes "sparrow" again, slower, looking at you. You let it. The kitchen god, beside you, very slightly leans against your wing.

choices.text: Answer with perfect courtesy, so the clerk looks like the rude one

ok.log: You bow, give your name and stage and the seven mansions of the south in order, and compliment the clerk on the ledger. The clerk turns pink, crosses out sparrow, and writes Vermilion Bird in a much better hand. The kitchen god is unbearable with pride all the way down.

fail.log: The courtesy comes out through your teeth. The clerk hears every tooth. You are written down as "sparrow, red, witness, rude", which is at least accurate.

choices.text: Let it out. Correct the clerk's ledger

effects.log: The ledger page where it says sparrow gently catches fire. Then the next. The clerk stares at it. The kitchen god covers its face with its apron. Two clerks run for water, and the whole outer office of heaven smells of burnt paper for a week. (Ash +1)

events.text: Back in the kitchen, on its shelf beside the bowl of clear water, the kitchen god tells you the verdict of heaven, which came down with the new year's smoke: the house is to have a good year, the rice will not burn, and the red bird is to be noted as "witness, satisfactory, do not invite again". The kitchen god seems pleased with all three.

choices.text: Wipe your feet on the edge of the shelf, for once

effects.log: The kitchen god watches you do it in total silence, and then, very carefully, refills its bowl of water from the jar, as if the occasion called for it. You think that is affection. It is hard to tell, with kitchen gods.

choices.text: Ask the kitchen god what it said about you, exactly

effects.log: "That you are hot-tempered, vain, and late," says the kitchen god. "And that this house has never been cold since you were born in it." It looks at you sideways. "Heaven only writes down the second part."

events.text: The south coast, and a bare hill above it with a beacon post on top: a walled yard, a hut for the soldiers, a storehouse of wolf dung and pine and rice straw, and five round stone chimneys in a row facing the sea. Every evening at dusk one fire is lit in the first chimney, and the next post along the coast lights one, and the next, all the way to the capital: one fire, nothing is wrong. Two, an enemy seen. Five, battle. You are the size of a crane now, and the chimney fits you as if it were built for you.

choices.text: Sit in the first chimney at dusk, and be the one fire

effects.log: The soldiers come up with their torch and find the chimney already burning, a tall clean fire that does not smoke. They stare at it. The next post along the coast sees it and lights its own. Nothing is wrong. You said so.

choices.text: Watch a season from the hut roof first, and learn the post

effects.log: Smoke by day, fire by night. Wolf dung for smoke that stands straight in the wind. The log of every evening's fire, sent up the coast. The soldiers' sore feet, their bored dice, their terror of lighting the wrong number. A beacon is a sentence the whole country reads. You learn its grammar.

choices.text: Look out at the sea, and think about what five fires would mean

effects.log: Five fires and the whole south takes up arms. Villages empty, the king wakes, soldiers march. A bird could do that with one breath. The thought sits in you, very warm, and you do not like how much you like it.

events.text: The captain of the beacon post, {npc}, is a lean, weathered soldier who has watched this sea for twenty years and says perhaps ten words a day. {npc} has noticed the chimney that lights itself. {He} has not reported it. Tonight {he} climbs up to the first chimney alone with a bowl of rice and sets it on the stone beside you, and sits down with {his} back to the chimney, facing the sea, as if you were another soldier on watch.

choices.text: Eat the rice, and watch the sea with {npc} until dawn

effects.log: All night, side by side, not a word. Near dawn {npc} points, once, at a light on the water: a fishing boat. You had seen it. You nod. {npc} nods. It is the beginning of the only kind of friendship either of you has ever been good at.

choices.text: Burn brighter, so {npc} knows you are no ordinary fire
