effects.log: {npc} looks up at the flame, then away at the sea again. "I know," {he} says. That is all. {He} leaves the rice. You eat it later, when nobody is looking.

events.text: The captain of the beacon post, {npc}, is a lean, weathered soldier with a face you know and cannot place, and then can: rain, dusk, a wet beacon pile that would not light, and a soldier deciding how many fires to set for sails on the horizon, who chose two, because two was what was truly seen. It cannot be the same soldier. That was another life. But {npc} looks up at the chimney that lights itself as if {he} had been waiting for it for a very long time.

choices.text: Burn two fires for a moment, and then one, so {npc} knows

mem.note: lit two fires for me, then one

effects.log: Two fires, in the empty sea dusk; then one. {npc} goes completely still. Then {he} laughs, a short surprised soldier's laugh. "What I truly saw," {he} says. "Yes." You trust this one. You do not know how you know.

choices.text: Sit beside {npc} and keep the watch, and say nothing about it

effects.log: All night, side by side. Some things are better not said. At dawn {npc} says, to the sea, "Two. It was two. I always wondered if anyone knew." You did.

events.text: Sails. Dusk, and rain sweeping in off the sea in grey curtains, and between two curtains, far out, low dark sails, seven or eight, coming in on the wind toward the islands. Then the rain closes again. {npc} is beside the chimney with a torch, soaked, and the wet pile in the second chimney will not take. {npc} looks at you. Fishing boats run for shelter before rain. So do raiders.

choices.text: Light two: an enemy seen. What you truly saw

effects.log: Two fires in the rain. Along the coast the posts light two, and the villages bar their gates and send the boats up the creeks. At dawn the sails are found burning nothing, beached and empty: raiders who saw the coast awake and went home. {npc} writes two in the log, and nothing else.

choices.text: Fly out over the sea in the rain and look before you light anything

ok.log: Low over the waves into the rain, and the sails are raiders, armed, with ladders. You come back to the hill like a thrown coal and light two, and then three. The coast is ready before the keels touch sand.

fail.log: An arrow out of the rain finds you over the third ship, and you come back to the hill hurt and late. {npc} has already lit two by hand. Good soldier. (-15 health)

choices.text: Light one. All is well. You are not sure, and five for nothing is worse

effects.log: One fire. {npc} looks at you and says nothing. At midnight, down the coast, a village goes up in flames, and the next post lights five, too late. In the morning {npc} goes down to help bury what can be buried, and does not speak to the chimney for a month.

events.text: The post's own fire is a poor thing: wolf dung and wet straw, lit every dusk with flint and swearing, and in the rains it fails one evening in five. {npc} has been to the commander's office twice to ask for better straw and been given worse. Tonight {he} stands in front of the first chimney with the flint in {his} hand and does not strike it. "You," {npc} says to the red bird on the chimney. "Every night. Will you?"

choices.text: Leave a fire of yours in the first chimney that will not go out

effects.log: A coal of you in the first chimney, banked in wolf-dung ash, that burns in any rain. {npc} tests it with a bucket of seawater, which you consider rude, and it burns on. One fire every evening, and the right number every night it matters. The Beacon burns, and {npc} keeps it.

choices.text: Leave it, and make {npc} promise the number will always be the truth

effects.log: {npc} promises with {his} hand on the cold stone of the chimney. A soldier's promise, ten words long. The coal of you in the first chimney flares once, as if it heard. The Beacon burns, and {npc} keeps it, and keeps the promise.

choices.text: Refuse. A beacon in the wrong hands empties a province

effects.log: You fly off the chimney. {npc} watches you go and strikes the flint, and the wet straw takes on the fourth try. You will think about this refusal later, when you need fires burning and this hill has none of yours.

events.text: Years of one fire every evening. {npc}'s child, then {npc}'s grandchild, carries the rice up to the first chimney now, and the log of the post is full of ones, page after page, with a two here and there, each of them true. Nobody on that coast can remember a raid that was not seen in time. {npc} is old and comes up the hill on a stick to sit with you at dusk.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} and watch the one fire go up the coast

effects.log: Post to post along the coast in the dusk, one fire, one fire, one fire, a line of small lights going north to the capital. "All is well," {npc} says, which is the most words {he} has said at once in a year. All is well.

choices.text: Burn two, just once, as a joke, and see {npc}'s face

effects.log: Two fires. {npc} drops the stick. Up the coast the next post lights two. You put it back to one at once, and spend the night flying up the coast relighting ones, and the log of the post has, for one evening, a two with a note beside it: "the bird". (Ash +1)

events.text: A new soldier at the beacon post, {npc}, young and quick and terrified of being the one who failed to see the enemy, is on watch alone at dusk when the fishing fleet comes home early, forty brown sails at once out of the haze. By the time you look up from the sea, {npc} has lit two chimneys from your fire, then three, and is running with the torch to the fourth. Five fires: battle. The next post along the coast is already lighting its second.

choices.text: Call your fire home out of the chimneys before the coast reads them

effects.log: You pull every flame on the hill back into your breast in one breath, all five, your own fire with them, and the hill goes dark. The next post sees darkness, and waits, and lights one. {npc} sits down in the dark and cries. The Beacon is out. You will have to give it again, and to someone steadier.

choices.text: Smother the fifth chimney with your own body before it takes

effects.log: You drop into the fifth chimney and lie on the fire like a hen on an egg, and it is the worst pain of your life, a fire that will not be put out pressing against a fire that will not go out. Four, then three as you beat the others down. The coast reads three, and runs, and comes back at dawn. (-20 health)

choices.text: Let it run. A coast that runs for nothing is still alive

effects.log: Five fires. All along the south coast, post after post, five fires go up and north into the night. By midnight the villages are on the roads with their cattle and their grandmothers. The capital wakes. And in the harbour below, forty fishing boats tie up and wonder where everyone went.

events.text: A new soldier at the beacon post, {npc}, is someone you somehow know: the one who, in a rain long ago and in another life, lit five fires so that the capital would listen. {npc} has the same face now, years younger, and the same fear. And at dusk the fishing fleet comes home early out of the haze, forty brown sails at once, and {npc} has the torch in the second chimney before you have finished turning your head.

choices.text: Call your fire home out of the chimneys before the coast reads them

effects.log: Every flame on the hill, back into your breast, and the hill goes dark. {npc} stands with the dead torch, shaking. "Again," {he} says. "I did it again." Not this time. The Beacon is out, and you will have to give it again.

choices.text: Take the torch out of {his} hand, gently, and light one

mem.note: took the torch from me and lit one

effects.log: Your beak closes on the torch and {npc} lets go of it, as if {he} had been waiting a long time for someone to. One fire. Two fires already lit go out under your wing. The coast reads one. {npc} sits down on the wall of the yard and does not move until dawn.

choices.text: Let it run

effects.log: Five fires, up the whole coast. {npc} watches them go north with a face you have seen before, in another life, in rain. Some people are made to light five. Some birds are made to let them.

events.text: The coast emptied for nothing. Three days on the roads in the spring rain: cattle lost, a granary looted by its own village's young men, an old woman who fell on the pass and broke her hip, rice seedlings left to rot in the beds. Now the villages are coming back down the hills, angry, and they want to know whose fire it was.

choices.text: Fly the roads and lead the stragglers home, one family at a time

effects.log: A red bird low over the muddy roads, going ahead of lost carts and lost children back to their own villages. By the end of the week the roads are empty. The anger is not. (-6 health)

choices.text: Sit on the beacon hill in plain sight. It was your fire

effects.log: The villagers come up the hill with sticks and see you on the chimney, the size of a crane and the colour of a burning house, and stop. They go down again. They do not stop blaming the bird. They are right to.

choices.text: Let them blame the soldier. The soldier lit it

effects.log: The villagers blame {npc}. Everyone blames {npc}. {npc} does not say a word about a bird, ever. You notice that, and it sits in you.

events.text: The inquiry. An inspector from the provincial army sits in the yard of the beacon post with the log open, and {npc} kneels on the stones in front of the table. The law is clear: a false fire is flogged, and a false five may be worse. The inspector is reading the entry for that evening for the third time, frowning at a note in the margin in {npc}'s hand: "the bird".

choices.text: Land on the table, on the open log, and look at the inspector

effects.log: The inspector looks at you for a long time. Then writes something in the log, closes it, and stands. "Weather," the inspector says. "A false fire caused by weather. Fifteen strokes for carelessness, not fifty." {npc} takes the fifteen without a sound and is back on watch in a week.

choices.text: Drop a fishing net float from the fleet at the inspector's feet

ok.log: A painted float with the fleet's mark. The inspector turns it over, understands, and laughs despite everything. "Forty sails out of the haze at dusk," the inspector says. "I would have lit three." Ten strokes.

fail.log: The inspector does not understand the float, or will not. Fifty strokes. {npc} is carried down the hill afterwards, and you sit on the chimney and burn very low for a month.

choices.text: Stay away. The soldier must answer for the soldier's own hand

effects.log: You watch from the sea cliff. {npc} answers for it, and is flogged, and does not mention you. Years later {npc} is the steadiest captain on the coast, and never once lights a fire without looking twice.

events.text: Years on, {npc} is captain of a beacon post of {his} own, up the coast, and is known from the islands to the capital as the slowest beacon in the south: never wrong, never early, and never once lit for anything but what was truly seen. Tonight, at dusk, a red bird lands on {his} first chimney, and {npc} looks up from the log.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} and keep the watch

effects.log: "I still dream about it," {npc} says, after an hour. "Forty sails." You know. You keep the watch together, and the sea is empty, and the fire on the chimney is one.

choices.text: Light a coal of yourself in {his} chimney, if {he} will have it

effects.log: "No," {npc} says, gently. "Not again. I will light my own." It is the right answer. You fly on up the coast, very pleased with a soldier, which is not something you expected. (-5 health)

events.text: Every evening your one fire goes up the coast and turns inland, post to post, hill to hill, a word passed hand to hand all the way to the capital. You have never seen where it ends. Tonight, when the first chimney is lit, you do not stay with it. You fly ahead of it, hill to hill, to watch each post light its one fire as yours comes into sight, and to see where the word goes.

choices.text: Fly the whole road in one night, as fast as the fire

ok.log: Hill, fire, hill, fire, through the mountains and over the rivers, a red bird racing a line of beacons north. You are faster. Just. At midnight you come over the last ridge, and below you is the capital.

fail.log: You are not faster. The beacons beat you to the capital by three hours, and you arrive at dawn, exhausted, with a wing that aches for a month. The word went without you. That is what words do. (-10 health)

choices.text: Fly it slowly over a month, and sit at every post

effects.log: Forty posts. A mountain post with a goat. A river post whose soldiers are all one family. A post where the captain is drunk and the cook keeps the fire. You come to the capital at the end of the month knowing the whole sentence, word by word.

events.text: The capital's southern hill. Five round beacon mounds in a row on its crown, where every road of fire in the kingdom ends, and soldiers who read them all night and send a runner down at dawn to the royal secretariat with the count. Below, the walled city and its tiled roofs and the palace, asleep. You perch on the first mound. The soldiers have never seen a bird on it before.

choices.text: Burn there one night, the fire that ends all the roads

effects.log: One fire on the southern hill, and it is you. Below, the city sleeps under it. The soldiers write in the log that the first mound burned red all night with no wood in it, and do not know what else to write.

choices.text: Sit beside the mound and watch the soldiers read the kingdom

effects.log: One from the south coast: yours. One from the east, one from the north, one from the west, one from the northwest. All is well, all is well, all is well. The soldiers yawn. It is the most peaceful thing you have ever seen, and it is made of fire.

events.text: In the royal secretariat, at dawn, the secretaries read the runner's count from the southern hill, and stop. Four roads report one fire, all is well. The southern road reports one fire, all is well, "burning red without wood, colour unknown, cause unknown." The chief secretary sends for the beacon log, and then for an astronomer, and then, because nobody knows what else to do, for the king.

choices.text: Sit on the secretariat roof and let them look at you

effects.log: The secretaries come out into the yard and look up at a red bird the size of a crane on their roof, and nobody says anything for a long time. The astronomer says something about the seven mansions of the south. The chief secretary writes it all down. It goes into the records of the court: a fire the beacons could not name.

choices.text: Fly home before the king is woken

effects.log: You are over the southern ridges before the palace gate opens. The secretaries write it down anyway: one fire, red, no wood, unknown. The court records keep it for five hundred years, unexplained, between a drought and a royal wedding.

choices.text: Burn one more night on the southern hill, so they know it was no mistake

effects.log: The second night the king himself comes up the southern hill in a chair to see the fire that burns red without wood. You burn for the king, straight and clean, one fire: all is well. He watches it until dawn and says nothing. It is the best thing a king has ever said to you.

events.text: Years later, a royal inspector comes down the beacon road to the south coast with a commission: find the red fire. The inspector is thorough. The inspector questions every captain on every post and climbs every hill, and comes at last to your beacon hill and finds an old captain, a log full of ones, and a coal in the first chimney that will not go out in seawater.

choices.text: Let the inspector see you, and bow, as one officer to another

effects.log: The inspector bows back, very correctly, and writes in the report: "The southern beacon is kept by a bird. The bird is courteous. Recommend no action." The court takes the recommendation. Somewhere in the capital there is a file with your name in it, and it is a good one.

choices.text: Stay out of sight. Let the captain answer for the post

effects.log: The old captain answers every question with as few words as possible, all true, none of them about you. The inspector goes home with a report that says the south coast beacon is the best kept in the kingdom, cause unknown.

events.text: Sails at dusk off the islands, not fishing sails: low dark ships with many oars, coming in fast on the evening tide toward a fishing village that has no wall. The beacon chain has seen them; two fires are going up the coast. But the village is between the ships and the hill, and the fishermen are still on the beach mending nets, looking the wrong way.

choices.text: Fly down over the village and set every dog barking

effects.log: You go down the beach like a falling torch, low over the huts, and every dog in the village goes mad, and the fishermen look up, and then out to sea, and run. By the time the keels touch sand the village is halfway up the hill with its children.

choices.text: Fly out to the ships and burn the lead ship's sail

roll.foeName: The raiders on the lead ship

ok.log: The sail goes up like paper. The lead ship swings broadside in the surf, and the ships behind it foul their oars on it. They land late, in the dark and scattered, and the village is already on the hill.

fail.log: Archers on the stern, more than you counted. You burn the sail and come away bleeding, and the ships land anyway, late. (-16 health)

events.text: The raiders are ashore. Torches in the thatch, the fishermen's huts going up one after another in the sea wind, a net shed, a boat on the sand, a granary: a fire that is not yours, set by people who want it to spread. It is spreading. And up on the hill, the village is watching its houses burn.

choices.text: Call the raiders' fire into yourself, hut by hut

effects.log: A fire that is not yours is hard to swallow; it fights you all the way down. Hut by hut the flames come away into your breast, until the village stands black and smoking but standing. You are hot inside for a season with a stranger's fire. (-14 health)

choices.text: Leave the huts. Guard the path up the hill where the children are

effects.log: You sit on the hill path, huge and burning, and the raiders who come up it after the children see you and go back down. The huts burn. Huts can be rebuilt. The village knows which was the right order.

choices.text: Turn their fire on their own ships

ok.log: You lift the burning thatch on the wind and lay it in the raiders' rigging. They run back to their ships to save them and lose half of them anyway. The ones who escape will not come to this coast again for years. It was still fire you set. (Ash +1)

fail.log: The wind turns. The fire you lifted comes down on the net sheds instead of the ships. More of the village burns, and some of it is your fire now. (Ash +1, -8 health)

events.text: Dawn on the beach. The raiders are going back to their ships, loaded with rice and cloth and three young fishermen roped together, and their captain, a big scarred raider with a curved blade, is the last off the sand. He turns, sees the red bird on the burnt boat, and laughs, and beckons: come on, then.

choices.text: Come down onto the sand and fight

ok.log: He is good. You are fire. The curved blade goes red in his hands and he drops it, and you stand over him in the surf until his own crew drag him into the boat. The three fishermen are left on the beach, untied. They will tell this story to their grandchildren.

fail.deathCause: a raider captain's blade on a burnt beach
fail.log: He is better than good. The blade catches your wing and you go down in the surf, and he laughs again, and goes. They take the fishermen. You lie in the surf with the sea hissing round you until the villagers come down. (-22 health)

choices.text: Go for the ropes, not the captain

ok.log: A burning dive past the captain's blade and the ropes part. Three fishermen run up the beach. The captain swears in two languages and wades out to his boat with nothing to show but rice.

fail.log: You burn one rope through. One fisherman runs. The captain's blade drives you off the other two. (-12 health)

choices.text: Let them go. You have done what a bird can

effects.log: The ships pull away with three young men aboard. You watch them from the burnt boat. It goes down into you, all of it, and stays.

events.text: Sails again at dusk off the islands, dark sails, many oars: the raiding season has come round. The beacon posts are lighting their twos up the coast, and in a dozen villages people are looking out to sea and then up at the sky, for a red bird.

choices.text: Fly to the village with no wall

effects.log: You get there first. The dogs bark, the boats go up the creek, the children up the hill. The raiders land on an empty beach, and you are on the ridge above it, burning, and they get back in their ships. (-6 health)

choices.text: Fight them at sea, before they land

ok.log: Two sails burned, one ship turned back on the reef. The rest decide this coast is not worth it this year.

fail.log: They have learned. Wet hides on the sails, archers in the bows. You come back to the beacon hill with an arrow-scar and the raiders land two bays down. (-16 health)

choices.text: Keep the watch from the beacon and trust the coast to do its part

effects.log: Two fires, then three, read right. The villages are ready. The army comes down the coast road in time. It is not as glorious as fighting. Nobody dies who did not have to.

events.text: {npc} lives alone in the ruin of a coast village that was never rebuilt, and rebuilds it, one hut a year, with {his} own hands, for nobody. The fishermen up the coast say {npc} was a beacon soldier once, who saw sails in the rain and lit one fire, all is well, because {he} was not sure; and the village burned. You know that story. In another life, it was the story of the soldier who lit one.

choices.text: Help {npc} rebuild: warm the clay, dry the thatch, every year

effects.log: Every year one more hut, and the clay dries faster than clay should, and the thatch never rots. After many years there are twenty huts, and a family moves in, and then another. {npc} never says a word about the bird. {He} leaves a bowl of rice on the beach every evening.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} on the beach at dusk and keep the watch

effects.log: "I was not sure," {npc} says to the sea, years into it. "One fire. I was not sure." You are not sure either, most days. You keep the watch together, and nothing comes.

choices.text: Light the ruin's old hearth again, the one that went out that night

effects.log: In the biggest ruin, the headman's house, the old hearth is cold under ten years of leaves. You light it, and keep it lit all winter. {npc} comes in at dusk, smells smoke, and stands in the doorway for a long time. Then {he} sits down by it. A fire for the one who lit one.

events.text: A letter comes down the river from the north in spring, with the snowmelt: an old tortoise shell, washed up on the black stones below the beacon hill, carved all over in two hands at once that run in opposite directions and say the same thing twice. It is addressed to the red bird of the south. It says, as far as you can read it, that fire and water must not touch, that your sparks have been seen in the north, and that the north would be obliged.

choices.text: Bow to the shell. The Black Tortoise is far older than you

effects.log: You bow to a letter on a riverbank, which feels foolish and is not. Then you read it again, both hands, very carefully. The north would be obliged. The north is extremely polite, and extremely cold, and has a long memory.

choices.text: Read it slowly, both hands, and find out which sparks

effects.log: One hand writes about the sparks; the other about the winter. A fire of yours, one given or one that got away, ran up a ridge and the smoke drifted north for three days, and the northern springs tasted of ash. You did not know. Fire goes further than you watch it.

choices.text: Laugh. Your sparks have been seen in the north

effects.log: You laugh, and the laugh is hot, and a corner of the carved shell blackens. A letter of the Black Tortoise, scorched. You stop laughing. You can feel, a thousand miles north, something very old making a note. (Ash +1)

events.text: You must reply. There is no shell in the south big enough to carve, so you burn your reply into a long board of pine with your beak, which takes all summer, and float it up the river on the autumn rains toward the north. What you say to the Black Tortoise is yours to decide.

choices.text: An apology: the sparks were yours, and you will watch them

effects.log: A plain apology burned into pine, without excuses. It takes much longer to write than an argument would. You float it north and feel, for a week, much smaller and much better.

choices.text: An argument: summer has always crossed into the north a little

effects.log: A very good argument, with the seasons and the mansions and the long habit of summer in it. You are rather proud of it. You float it north. The Black Tortoise will take a hundred years to answer, and will win.

choices.text: A song, burned in as notes, about the warmth the north never asked for

effects.log: A song in pine, about spring melt and a red bird and a letter in two hands. It is not an answer. It is better. You float it north on the rains, and do not know if a tortoise sings.

events.text: Years on, a second shell comes down the river with the snowmelt. One hand on it says your reply was received. The other hand says it was read, which is not the same thing. Both hands together, at the very end, in letters so small you nearly miss them, say that the youngest of the Four always writes too much, and that the north remembers when it, too, was young.

choices.text: Keep the shell on the beacon hill, where the sea can see it

effects.log: The youngest of the Four. You had not thought of yourself as one of the Four at all. You sit by the shell all evening and look north, where the oldest of them is, very slowly, being kind.

choices.text: Write back at once. Too much

effects.log: Twice as long as the first reply. You know it is too much while you burn it. You float it north anyway. Somewhere in the north, you are almost sure, something very old will be amused.

events.text: Somewhere under your breast, all these years, one feather has stayed grey: the colour of the ash you were born in, small and soft and stubborn, hidden under the red. This spring, preening on the beacon chimney, you find it loose. It would come out with one pull.

choices.text: Pull it out and let it go on the wind

effects.log: It goes down the hill on the sea wind, turning over and over, grey against the blue, until you cannot see it. Every feather on you now is the colour of fire. You feel, for a moment, lighter than you should.

choices.text: Leave it. It will fall when it falls

effects.log: You preen round it. A grey feather under the red, the last of the chick in the fire jar. It can stay a while longer.

choices.text: Pull it out and carry it to the fire jar you were born in

effects.log: A long flight north for one grey feather. The youngest of the house is a great-grandparent now and does not see you come down the chimney. You leave it in the ash of the fire jar. (-3 health)

events.text: The last grey feather has fallen, wherever it fell. You are vermilion now from beak to tail, the colour of cinnabar and summer and the south wall of a painted tomb, with a tail that has grown long and curls in the wind like smoke. The beacon soldiers have stopped saying "the bird" and started saying "the Bird". The children on the coast draw you on walls with burnt sticks, and get the tail wrong, and it is still you.

choices.text: Fly along the whole coast once, slowly, so everyone can see

effects.log: From the islands to the capes, low over the villages, every head turning up. You are vain about it. You are entitled, for one day.

choices.text: Look at yourself in the still water of a pond, a long time

effects.log: A vermilion bird in the pond, burning, with a whirlwind tail. You look for the grey chick in it and cannot find it, and then, in the eyes, you can.

events.text: A valley in the south with good water and a mountain at its back, and a geomancer walking it with a compass on a cord: {npc}, old, thin, in a hat with a frayed brim, who has been hired by three families to find them a site. The back mountain is right. The ridges on the left and right are right. But the hill to the south, the one the houses must face, the one that should shield the site and break the river's rush, is bare and dull and has no life in it. {npc} is shaking {his} head.

choices.text: Settle on the facing hill, and let the life come into it

effects.log: You come down on the crown of the bare hill and fold your wings, and the hill warms under you like a hearthstone. By evening the grass on it is greener. {npc} has stopped shaking {his} head and is staring, compass forgotten, at a hill that has a bird on it.

choices.text: Fly over the valley first and see it as {npc} sees it

effects.log: The back mountain like a seated elder. The left ridge, the right ridge, arms round the site. The river coming in fast from the west. And the south hill, where something should be, and nothing is. You understand at once. You go and be it.

choices.text: Leave the valley to its geomancer. A hill is not a fire

effects.log: You fly on. Behind you {npc} tells the three families to look in the next valley. Some valleys wait a long time for a hill to wake up.

events.text: Dawn over the valley, and {npc} the geomancer has climbed the back mountain to look south at the site one last time before the families decide. You are on the facing hill. The sun comes up behind you and something in you wants to rise with it, and turn, and spread every feather you have against the light. Below, the old geomancer has the compass in one hand and the book of the art in the other, open to a page.

choices.text: Rise and dance on the wind above the hill, all the way through the dawn

effects.log: You soar, and turn, and fall, and soar, a long red tail curling behind you like a whirlwind, until the sun is up. When you land, {npc} is sitting on the back mountain with the book in {his} lap, open at an old phrase: the vermilion bird soaring and dancing. "Here," {npc} tells the families. "Build here. Face the bird."

choices.text: Stay still on the crown of the hill, a guardian, not a dancer

effects.log: You sit as still as the hill, burning, while the sun comes up. {npc} looks a long time. "Soaring and dancing, the book says," {npc} mutters. "Well. Sitting will do." The families build.

events.text: The houses go up facing you. Three families, then six, every house turned south so that its doors and its verandas and the eyes of everyone sitting on them look out across the valley at your hill. On the day the headman's ridge-pole is raised, with rice cakes and wine and a cloth tied to the beam, the whole village turns at the end of the rite and bows, not to the headman, but south.

choices.text: Bow back, from the hill, so the whole valley sees it

effects.log: A vermilion bird on a hill, bowing to a village. The children talk of nothing else for a year. The elders say it was courtesy, and that the south is known for it, and that it bodes well. It does.

choices.text: Burn a little higher on the hill, warmly, and stay seated

effects.log: That winter is the mildest anyone in the valley can remember. The hill does not freeze. The village thinks that is what a good site does. It is.

choices.text: Feel the weight of every pair of eyes facing you, and be afraid of it

effects.log: Every door in the valley open toward you. Every child taught to bow south. If you burned, they would see it from their own verandas. You stay on the hill, and you do not burn, and you understand for the first time what it means to be the thing a place faces.

events.text: Spring flood. The river comes into the valley from the west fat with snowmelt and rain, the colour of tea, and fast, straight at the new houses, the way the geomancer said it would without a hill to turn it. The facing hill is what turns it. You are the facing hill. The water is climbing its foot.

choices.text: Hold the hill's foot against the river with your whole heat

ok.log: Fire against water, all night, at the foot of the hill: steam like a second river. At dawn the flood has bent round the hill the long way and gone down the valley slowly, as a river should. The houses stand. The paddies have mud on them, not water.

fail.log: The water is stronger than heat. It takes the lowest paddies and one barn before it turns. Nobody drowns. You are cold to the bone, and you lie on the hill all spring getting warm again. (-18 health)

choices.text: Fly the valley and get the families onto the hill itself

effects.log: Up onto the hill, the old and the children first, the cattle after. The flood takes the paddies and half the barns. The families sit on the warm grass of your hill all night, and nobody is cold, and nobody drowns.

events.text: Long years on, and the valley is a village of forty houses that all face south, and a school, and a pavilion on the facing hill where the old men sit in summer. Every new year's morning the whole village comes out onto the verandas and bows to the hill before it bows to its own elders. The geomancer's grandchild, a geomancer too, brings students to look at the site, and tells them it is the best-faced valley in the south, and why.

choices.text: Be the hill. Let them bow

effects.log: You sit through the new years on the hill. The village grows old facing you, and young again, and old. It is the longest you have stayed anywhere since the fire jar. It feels like the fire jar.

choices.text: Sit in the old men's pavilion on a summer night, among them

effects.log: The old men pretend not to see a vermilion bird on the pavilion rail. One of them pours a second cup and sets it down by your feet, and goes on with his story about a tax collector. You stay until the cup is empty.

events.text: The house you were born in. The fire jar is the same, cracked and mended twice. The youngest of the house who first knelt and blew on you is long dead, and so are their children, and the one banking the jar tonight is {npc}, fifteen, a great-grandchild, yawning, doing it all wrong: too little ash, the lid askew, a careless knock on the side of the jar. You are on the ridge-pole, and you find, tonight, that you can speak.

choices.text: "Not like that."

mem.note: told me from the ridge-pole how to bank the fire jar

effects.log: Your first words to a human, in a voice like a coal settling: a scolding about the fire jar. {npc} drops the lid. Then picks it up, and banks the jar properly, very carefully, without once looking up. You have never been so proud of anything.

choices.text: "More ash on the left. It burns faster on the left."

effects.log: A whole sentence, practical, perfectly polite. {npc} does exactly as told, and then sits back on {his} heels and says, to the kitchen in general, "Who said that?" You do not answer. You are enjoying it too much.

choices.text: Say nothing. Words are a door, and it opens both ways

effects.log: You stay silent. {npc} bangs the jar again on the way out. In the morning the fire is low and sulky, and so are you.

events.text: {npc} has worked out where the voice comes from, and has climbed onto the kitchen roof at dusk with a bowl of rice and a great many questions. Why the ridge-pole. Why the fire jar. Whether you are the thing great-grandmother said lived in it, the thing that chirps. Whether it is true that if the fire goes out the luck of the house goes with it.

choices.text: Answer every question, truthfully, until the rice is gone

effects.log: Yes, the ridge-pole. Yes, the jar. Yes, the chirping. No, the luck of the house is the people in it. {npc} listens with {his} mouth open and forgets to eat, so you eat the rice.

choices.text: Answer one question, and make {npc} earn the next

effects.log: One answer for a properly banked jar. One for clean water in the kitchen god's bowl. One for a winter of not knocking the jar. By spring {npc} is the best fire-keeper the house has had in a hundred years, and has learned four things about you.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the luck is in the fire, so {he} will keep it carefully

effects.log: It is not quite a lie. {npc} keeps the jar like a holy thing from that night on. It is not quite the truth either, and you know which part you left out.

events.text: {npc} is grown, with a child of {his} own who is banking the fire jar tonight, badly, while {npc} watches from the door with folded arms and looks up, past the eaves, at the ridge-pole. "Well?" {npc} says. "Are you going to tell the child, or shall I?"

choices.text: "You tell the child. It is your house."

effects.log: {npc} kneels and shows the child, word for word, the way you told it on the first night: more ash on the left. You listen from the ridge-pole. It is the strangest thing, to hear your first words come back to you in someone else's mouth.

choices.text: "Not like that," you say to the child, as you said to {npc}

effects.log: The child drops the lid. {npc} laughs out loud in the doorway, a laugh you have not heard since {npc} was fifteen. The child banks the jar properly, very carefully, without looking up.

events.text: A great rite in a village by the sea: three days of drums, the offering table piled with rice cakes and fruit and a pig's head, and the shaman {npc} dancing the five directions in a red robe with a fan in one hand and bells in the other, calling each guardian in turn. East, west, north, the centre. Then {npc} turns south, and stops dead, the fan raised, the bells silent, and calls for the bird of summer to come down.

choices.text: Come down onto the shrine roof

effects.log: The drums stop. The whole village looks up. {npc} does not look up: {npc} has known for three days that you were on the ridge, and only bows, with the red fan, to the south. You have been called, and you came. The rite goes on until dawn, and it is about you now.

choices.text: Answer from the dark with one flare of heat, and stay hidden

effects.log: Every candle on the offering table flares up at once. The village gasps. {npc} smiles very slightly and goes on dancing. A call answered, and nothing shown that did not need showing.

choices.text: Do not answer. You are not a thing to be summoned with a fan

effects.log: You stay on the ridge. {npc} stands facing south with the fan raised for a long, long time, and then lowers it, and goes on, and the village does not notice. {npc} does. So do you.

events.text: {npc} the shaman comes to the shrine at the edge of the village at dusk, alone, and lights no candle, and speaks to the dark. The rites of the lineages on this coast have gone wrong, {npc} says: the candles at the ancestral tablets gutter on the night of the rite, the dead come to the wrong houses, a grandfather has been seen in a stranger's kitchen. The rite candle wants a fire that knows where the dead belong. "Yours," {npc} says. "Red. The yang colour."

choices.text: Give the shrine a Rite Candle of your own fire

effects.log: One candle on the shrine's altar, red-flamed, that burns all year and does not shorten. On the night of the rites the dead come, and go to the right houses, and leave before cockcrow. {npc} keeps it, and trims it, and talks to it. The Rite Candle burns, and {npc} keeps it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the dead want, first

effects.log: "To be remembered in order," {npc} says. "Eldest first. Nobody forgotten. Nobody pushed in front." It is a matter of courtesy, then. You understand courtesy. You will think about it.

choices.text: Refuse. Fire for the living is enough work

effects.log: {npc} bows, and lights an ordinary candle, and the rites go on going wrong, a little. You hear about the grandfather in the stranger's kitchen for years.

events.text: The night of the autumn rites. In every house on the coast the tablets are set out and the food laid in the old order, and in the shrine your Rite Candle burns red and steady. Near midnight something comes up the road that is not on any tablet: a cold, wet, angry thing, a drowned sailor nobody remembers, going from door to door and finding no place set for it.

choices.text: Light the drowned one's way to the shrine, and have a place set

effects.log: {npc} sets a bowl of rice on the shrine step for a sailor with no name, and the cold thing comes up the road following a red light and sits by the bowl until cockcrow, and goes. Nobody pushed in front. Nobody forgotten.

choices.text: Drive it off with red, the yang colour

ok.log: You flare red across the road and the cold thing flinches back into the sea mist and is gone. The rites go on in order. {npc} watches the road a long time afterward, as if sorry for it.

fail.log: It is colder than you thought. It goes through you like a wave through a lantern, and you sit in the shrine shaking until dawn. The candle holds. (-10 health)

events.text: The hearth of the house you first warmed has burned sixty years without being made new. Tonight the fire jar cracks with a sound like a slap, and the fire comes out of it onto the kitchen floor, and up the doorpost, and into the thatch, quick and bright and glad to be out. The swallows bring it to you on the wind before the house is awake.

choices.text: Race there with the season's wood and rub it new before it runs

ok.log: You come down on the house with green wood in your claws and rub new fire in the middle of the old, and the old lets go of the world and comes back to you, all of it, in one long breath. By dawn the Hearth burns small and young where it belongs. The people who saw it will talk about the night the fire changed its mind.

effects.log: The next spring {npc} walks to the kiln hill on the southwest coast and stands at a spy-hole through a whole firing. {He} comes home with no eyebrows and tears up the treatise and starts again.

events.text: The newest member of a house, {npc}, married in this spring from a village across the hills, is being blamed. Every morning the fire jar is cold, and every morning the household says it was {npc}'s night to bank it, and the mother-in-law has begun to say things about luck. You know why the jar is cold. A rat under the kitchen floor has been stealing the embers for its nest.

choices.text: Tell {npc}, at dusk, from the ridge: "Look under the floor."

mem.note: told me from the roof where the embers went

effects.log: {npc} takes up a floorboard with the whole household watching and finds a rat's nest lined with black coals and one still-red ember. The mother-in-law says nothing for a full day, which in that house is an apology.

choices.text: Tell the mother-in-law instead, loudly, from the ridge

effects.log: The mother-in-law hears a voice from the roof, which says some things about luck and rats and new members of houses, and goes to bed for two days, and gets up much kinder to {npc}, and very nervous of the roof.

choices.text: Deal with the rat yourself, and tell no one

effects.log: You go down the chimney at midnight and have a word with the rat, the way you did with another rat long ago. It moves out. The fire jar stays warm. Nobody ever knows why, and {npc} is blamed for nothing ever again, and never learns why that is either.

events.text: A child, {npc}, about eight, has climbed onto the roof of the family house in the evening by way of the persimmon tree, as you once did, and has crept along the ridge to sit right beside you, and is looking at your wings with the most serious face you have ever seen. "Teach me to fly," {npc} says.

choices.text: "No. But I will sit here while you climb down."

effects.log: You sit on the ridge, warm and bright, so {npc} can see every tile, until {npc} is safe on the persimmon branch, and then on the ground, and then indoors being shouted at. {npc} comes back up the next evening. You sit there again.

choices.text: Tell {npc} how you learned: into the soy jar, onto the roof

effects.log: Into the soy-sauce jar, out of it, onto the persimmon, onto the ridge, sticky and singed. {npc} laughs so hard {he} nearly falls off, and you put out a wing, and {he} does not. Some lessons are only stories. That is the right kind.

events.text: A carpenter, {npc}, is raising the ridge-pole of a new house today: the great beam hoisted onto the posts, a cloth tied round it, the date written on its underside, rice cakes and wine on a table below for the household gods. And {npc}, with everyone watching, has turned to the vermilion bird on the neighbour's roof, and bowed, and asked, "Will you bless the beam?"

choices.text: Land on the new ridge-pole and sit there a moment

effects.log: You come across onto the new beam, and it creaks, and holds, and is warm where you sat. The household cheers. {npc} writes, under the date on the beam's underside, a little red bird. That house is never cold.

choices.text: "Write the date straight, and it will not need me."

effects.log: {npc} looks at the date and finds it written crooked, and goes very red, and writes it again. The household thinks it was a blessing anyway. It was, in a way.

events.text: Nets on the kiln ridge: silk this time, fine as mist, strung between bamboo poles across the path you fly at dawn, with lime on the twigs at either end and two cinnabar hunters crouched in the wet grass with a cage. They think you have not seen them. You have been watching them set it since midnight.

choices.text: Fly straight through and burn it as you go

ok.log: The silk goes up like a fuse along its whole length, and the hunters roll out of the grass with their eyebrows gone. You are over the ridge before the cage hits the ground.

fail.log: Silk over wire. It holds a breath too long and the lime takes three feathers. Somebody will be very rich from those three feathers. (-12 health)

choices.text: Take the long way round the ridge, and let them wait

effects.log: You go round by the sea. They wait all day in the wet grass. At dusk they pack up and go home, and you hear one of them say he is going back to selling salt.

events.text: On the beacon path at dusk there is a red bird in a cage: a hen, dyed with cinnabar, with a coal tied in a little clay pot to its leg so it glows. It is clucking miserably. The bird-catcher who set it is in the bushes, and has heard that a red bird of the south cannot pass one of its own kind in trouble.

choices.text: Free the hen, and let the bird-catcher try

ok.log: The cage door, the clay pot, the hen running off down the path, and the bird-catcher's net closing on empty air where you were. The hen lives with a farmer on the coast for years, slightly pink.

fail.log: The net comes down as you lift the cage door. You burn out of it, and the hen goes free, and you leave half a tail feather behind. (-10 health)

choices.text: Leave it. It is a trap, and a hen

effects.log: You fly past. It is a trap and a hen. It is also a frightened thing in a cage with a coal tied to its leg, and you think about it all night.

choices.text: Laugh. It is a hen

effects.log: You laugh, and the dye on the hen catches, a little, and the hen runs off clucking and smoking into the dusk. The bird-catcher comes out of the bushes and stares after it. You are already gone. (Ash +1)
